text:
On a donné un objectif de livraison en début d’année, il reste valable. Après un premier trimestre plus difficile, le deuxième s’est révélé excellent, et l’outil industriel est bien chargé : nos fournisseurs livrent ce qu’ils doivent livrer. On vise donc toujours environ 870 avions livrés cette année, ce qui nous ramènerait au niveau de 2019, juste avant la pandémie. Nous avons pour ambition un rythme de 75 avions par mois fin 2027, sans être certain d’y arriver à cette date précise. Le vrai objectif, c’est d’arriver à cette cadence sur plusieurs années tout en passant d’une forte production d’A320 avant pandémie à une très forte production d’avions A321.

C’est-à-dire ?

Avant la crise du Covid, notre outil productif de monocouloirs était surtout calibré pour le modèle A320. Quatre de nos huit chaînes d’assemblages pouvaient produire uniquement l’A320. Aujourd’hui, nous comptons dix chaînes d’assemblage dédiées au modèle A321neo. La demande est très forte pour cet avion qui a très peu de concurrence et offre une meilleure performance par siège et par kilomètre. Notre carnet de commandes total approche les 10 000 avions – un niveau inédit –, dont 8 000 pour la seule famille des monocouloirs [majoritairement des A321neo, NDLR], qui nous donne une grande visibilité et la capacité d’investir dans la durée.

Comment concilier cette montée en cadence avec l’objectif de neutralité carbone de l’aviation en 2050 ?

Depuis les années 1960, on a réduit de 80 % les émissions de carbone par passager et par kilomètre, ce qui a permis de garder stable la part de l’aviation dans les émissions mondiales de CO2, autour de 2 à 2,5 %, malgré le doublement du trafic tous les quinze ans. Le principal levier restant, c’est la production de carburant d’aviation durable, le SAF [Sustainable Aviation Fuel, un carburant alternatif non fossile, NDLR]. Sur ce point, la montée en cadence n’est pas suffisante et l’environnement international freine la dynamique de production. Concernant la partie avion, on est en ligne avec nos objectifs 2050 ; pour la partie carburants, on a pris du retard qu’il faut rattraper.

« Il ne faut surtout pas croire que ce qui s’est passé dans d’autres industries, comme l’automobile, ne puisse pas arriver dans la nôtre »

Où en est l’avion de nouvelle génération, prévu pour un lancement en 2030 ?

Sa consommation de carburant sera réduite de 20 à 25 %, voire 30 %, par rapport à celle d’un A321neo. Une performance réalisée pour moitié grâce à la propulsion, pour moitié grâce à l’avion lui-même : des ailes beaucoup plus longues et plus légères, un travail poussé sur les matériaux et l’aérodynamique et des moteurs à plus grand diamètre de soufflante. Nous tablons sur une entrée en service dès la deuxième moitié de la prochaine décennie. L’avion nouvelle génération, ce sera d’ici onze ou douze ans donc.

Comment jugez-vous la concurrence chinoise, qui monte en puissance ?

Il ne faut surtout pas croire que ce qui s’est passé dans d’autres industries, comme l’automobile, ne puisse pas arriver dans la nôtre. Les Chinois ont aujourd’hui un avion en service, avec une quarantaine d’exemplaires en vol, équivalents à la génération de l’A320. Nous sommes, nous, dans celle des A321. La vraie course se jouera sur la génération suivante : c’est pour cela que nous nous concentrons sur sa préparation, pour garder de l’avance, sachant qu’ils iront vite.

Vous êtes aussi un acteur majeur de la défense et du spatial. Ou en est le projet de rapprochement entre Airbus, Thales et Leonardo, baptisé Bromo ?

Airbus est le premier acteur de défense de l’Union européenne, le militaire représentant près de 20 % de notre chiffre d’affaires. En Europe, on dépense trop peu et de façon trop fragmentée dans le spatial par rapport aux États-Unis, à la Chine ou à l’Inde. Avec Thales et Leonardo, nous travaillons donc au rapprochement de nos activités spatiales pour retrouver l’effet d’échelle indispensable à la compétitivité et à l’investissement. Notre objectif est de créer cette nouvelle entreprise d’ici la fin de l’année prochaine.

En 2025, en France, nous avons recruté 3 200 personnes. Nous recrutons en moyenne 10 000 personnes par an dans le monde, dont un tiers en France et un autre tiers en Allemagne

En pleine campagne présidentielle, quelle mesure aimeriez-vous voir émerger dans le débat public ?

Il n’y a pas une mesure magique : la compétitivité est le résultat d’un ensemble de facteurs, coût de l’énergie, coût de la main-d’œuvre et surtout lourdeur réglementaire. Quand il faut cinq ans pour monter un site industriel en France contre deux aux États-Unis, la tentation d’aller outre-Atlantique est très forte. Nous avons besoin d’une vision européenne cohérente et d’une simplification réglementaire, sans quoi, face à des concurrents plus rapides, nous finirons par perdre.

Que représente la Nouvelle-Aquitaine pour Airbus aujourd’hui, et de nouveaux investissements sont-ils prévus dans la région, après ceux de Rochefort ?

Nous comptons un peu moins de 2 000 collaborateurs en Nouvelle-Aquitaine. Ce n’est certes pas notre premier bassin d’emploi, contrairement à l’Occitanie ou à la région Paca, mais nous y restons un acteur important. À Rochefort, en Charente-Maritime, nous venons de mettre en service une extension de 2 000 mètres carrés réservée à la production tout juste livrée pour soutenir la montée en cadence de l’A350. Un nouveau bâtiment de 8 000 mètres carrés y est également en construction, destinée à la fabrication de fauteuils passagers Business et First Class commercialisés sous la marque Stelia Aerospace. Sa livraison est prévue au printemps 2027.

En termes de créations d’emplois, après de très nombreux recrutements post-Covid, quels sont les niveaux de recrutements à venir pour Airbus ?

Pour Airbus, cette année, on est dans une continuité par rapport aux années précédentes sachant qu’en 2025, nous avons recruté 3 200 personnes. À l’échelle du groupe, ces dernières années, nous avons recruté 10 000 personnes par an dans le monde… Dont un tiers en France et un autre tiers en Allemagne.

text:
An unnamed energy company plans to work with Chinese pyrolysis technology provider Niutech on a refinery upgrade to turn waste plastic into material for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), potentially helping to tackle rising plastic waste and the aviation industry's push for cleaner fuel.

Under a new deal, an unnamed energy company will work with Chinese pyrolysis technology provider Niutech to install an industrial-scale unit that turns waste plastic into material for sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF.

Here's what to know

According to Interesting Engineering, the plan is to add the system to an existing refinery, linking plastic-waste treatment with hydrotreated SAF production so that discarded plastic can move through a single chain into jet-fuel ingredients.

Niutech's system uses continuous pyrolysis, heating plastic with limited oxygen so it breaks down into hydrocarbon products such as pyrolysis oil. That oil can then be further refined into SAF. The planned production line will have a single-unit capacity of about 11,023 to 55,116 US tons per year (10,000 to 50,000 metric tons per year).

One notable aspect of the system is the range of plastics Niutech said it can process. The company said it can handle plastics such as polypropylene, polyethylene, polystyrene, acrylonitrile butadiene styrene, and nylon, either individually or in mixed streams.

Mixed and contaminated plastic waste is often difficult and expensive to recycle. If a commercial system can avoid extensive washing, sorting, and drying, it could lower processing costs and make it easier to handle plastic that might otherwise end up in landfills, incinerators, or nearby communities as pollution.

More background

The agreement comes as airlines and fuel producers race to expand SAF supply. Under the EU's ReFuelEU Aviation rules, SAF must account for 2% of fuel supplied at EU airports in 2025, rising to 6% in 2030 and 70% by 2050.

Used cooking oil and similar waste oils are established SAF feedstocks, but supply remains constrained. Waste plastic could offer another source of hydrocarbons, particularly for facilities already equipped to refine fuel at scale.

Better systems for handling low-value plastic waste could ease pressure on local waste streams, reduce pollution risks, and support cleaner air by displacing some fossil-based inputs in aviation fuel production.

Niutech also said it has deployed continuous pyrolysis systems in the United Kingdom, South Korea, Denmark, Thailand, Vietnam, and China, with multiple projects already delivering roughly 11,023 US tons per year (10,000 metric tons per year).

What's being done?

The agreement is aimed at integrating the technology into a refinery setting rather than treating plastic-to-fuel as a small pilot project, where continuous operation is essential to both output and economics.

If successful, the project could open a larger commercial market for harder-to-recycle plastics while giving fuel producers another way to meet SAF targets. In practical terms, that could help diversify supply and potentially ease some of the cost pressure tied to limited feedstocks.

Still, it is not a replacement for reducing unnecessary plastic use in the first place. Households can continue cutting waste and saving money by choosing reusable goods and choosing plastic-free options for everyday products when possible.

The next major test will be whether waste plastic-to-SAF systems can run reliably, make economic sense, and perform at industrial scale. If they can, this refinery upgrade could point to a future in which more discarded plastic is put to use instead of piling up as pollution.

Where can I learn more?

This refinery plan is part of a broader push to find better uses for plastic that conventional recycling often can't handle. Other reporting and research in this space follow new fuel pathways, emerging chemical processes, and the bigger question of what to do with low-value waste that keeps piling up.

• Scientists have shown that powerful clean fuel from plastic waste could help power hydrogen cars.

• At Virginia Tech, engineers are advancing breakthroughs that could revolutionize how plastic gets reused.

• At the University of Texas, lasers may permanently change plastic by recovering reusable chemicals.

• Greenpeace argues plastic recycling is a failed concept as U.S. waste keeps rising.

That wider backdrop helps explain why plastic-to-SAF is getting attention as traditional recycling continues to fall short. It also highlights the big question behind all of these efforts: whether newer conversion technologies can move beyond the lab and work at commercial scale.

Chennai, Sep 5 (IANS) Actor, producer and parliamentarian Kamal Haasan has now congratulated the team of director Girish AD's recently released blockbuster Malayalam film 'Bethlehem Kudumba Unit', featuring actors Nivin Pauly and Mamitha Baiju in the lead.

Mythri Movie Makers, the production house that is distributing the film in the Telugu states, on Saturday released a video clip of the core team of the film calling on Kamal Haasan.

It wrote, "A SPECIAL MOMENT FOR TEAM #BethlehemKudumbaUnit! Ulaganayagan @ikamalhaasan garu met the team and congratulated them on the blockbuster success #BKUTelugu In Cinemas Now! Book Your Tickets Now. Telugu States Release by @MythriReleases."

The clip released showed Kamal Haasan warmly welcoming the 'Bethlehem Kudumba Unit' team led by one of its producers Fahadh Faasil. The team was seen having a conversation with Kamal Haasan after which each of the team members got a photo of themselves clicked with the star.

For the unaware, the film has emerged a roaring blockbuster, already collecting over Rs 200 crores worldwide.

It may be recalled that the makers of the film had recently appealed to the public not to record or share theatre snippets and key scenes of the film on social media.

Bhavana Studios, the production house that has distributed the film, issued a statement, which actor Nivin Pauly had shared on his social media timelines. Sharing the statement of the production house, the actor had said, "Request your attention!"

In its statement, the production house had said, "Thank you for the global blockbuster love! We're overwhelmed by the unprecedented bookings and the incredible joy you're bringing to theatres."

It then made a request. The production house said, "A humble request: Kindly avoid recording or sharing theatre snippets and key scenes on social media. Let everyone experience the magic and surprises of the film on the big screen. Let's keep the experience special for everyone. See you at the theatres!"

The film, which hit screens worldwide on August 21 this year, has gone on to emerge a massive blockbuster.

The story of the film has been penned by director Girish AD along with Kiran Josey.

Cinematography for the film is by Ajmal Sabu while music for the film has been scored by Vishnu Vijay. Akash Joseph Varghese was the editor for the film, which was distributed by Bhavana.

Production for the film, which Nivin Pauly had said was going to be "very special", had kicked off in September last year.

Bhavana Studios is a company partnered by director Dileesh Pothan, actor Fahadh Faasil and scenarist Syam Pushkaran.

text:
Ketahanan energi dan transisi energi menjadi salah satu isu strategis yang dibawa PT Pertamina (Persero) dalam gelaran IdeaFest 2026. Di hadapan generasi muda yang memiliki peran penting dalam membentuk masa depan Indonesia, Pertamina memperkenalkan Dual Growth Strategy, strategi perusahaan untuk memperkuat bisnis energi eksisting sekaligus mengembangkan bisnis rendah karbon sebagai sumber pertumbuhan baru.

Corporate Secretary Pertamina, Arya Dwi Paramita, menyampaikan strategi tersebut dalam sesi IdeaFest 2026 di Jakarta Convention Center (JCC) Senayan, Jakarta, Jumat (4/9/2026). Menurutnya, forum seperti IdeaFest menjadi ruang penting untuk membuka wawasan generasi muda mengenai tantangan energi sekaligus mendorong lahirnya gagasan dan inovasi untuk menjawab kebutuhan energi masa depan.

Arya menjelaskan, sebagai perusahaan energi nasional, Pertamina memiliki peran strategis dalam menjaga ketahanan energi Indonesia. Tantangannya, konsumsi energi nasional saat ini masih lebih tinggi dibandingkan kemampuan produksi dalam negeri sehingga sebagian kebutuhan masih harus dipenuhi melalui impor.

“Sudah lama sekali kita melakukan impor. Artinya, konsumsi kita lebih tinggi daripada produksi nasional. Di situlah kita perlu mendatangkan pasokan migas dari negara lain untuk memenuhi kebutuhan dalam negeri,” ujar Arya.

Menurut Arya, kondisi tersebut menjadi salah satu tantangan yang perlu dijawab melalui penguatan produksi dalam negeri sekaligus pengembangan sumber energi baru. Karena itu, Pertamina menjalankan Dual Growth Strategy dengan dua fokus yang berjalan beriringan, yakni mengoptimalkan bisnis eksisting untuk memenuhi kebutuhan energi masyarakat serta mengembangkan bisnis rendah karbon untuk masa depan.

“Untuk memenuhi kebutuhan saat ini, kita harus menjaga ketahanan produksi agar masyarakat tetap mendapatkan BBM. Di sisi lain, kita juga membangun bisnis rendah karbon dan energi baru terbarukan ,” jelasnya.

Pada bisnis rendah karbon, Pertamina terus mengembangkan berbagai potensi energi terbarukan dan teknologi rendah karbon, antara lain panas bumi, energi surya, serta bahan bakar penerbangan berkelanjutan atau Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF).

Salah satu inovasi yang telah dikembangkan adalah pemanfaatan used cooking oil (UCO) atau minyak jelantah sebagai bahan baku SAF. Minyak jelantah yang dikumpulkan kemudian diolah di Kilang Pertamina Cilacap bersama bahan baku pendukung lainnya hingga menghasilkan bahan bakar penerbangan rendah karbon.

“Minyak itu kita buat untuk bahan bakar pesawat udara. Namun jangan khawatir, ini aman karena risetnya sudah diinisiasi sejak 2015, diteliti secara ketat dan diuji coba dari 2021 hingga 2025,” kata Arya.

SAF berbasis minyak jelantah tersebut juga telah digunakan dalam penerbangan Pelita Air Service, anak perusahaan Pertamina, pada rute Jakarta–Bali.

Arya menegaskan, pengembangan berbagai inovasi tersebut menunjukkan bahwa transisi energi berjalan beriringan dengan upaya menjaga ketahanan energi nasional. Pertamina tetap memperkuat bisnis energi eksisting untuk memenuhi kebutuhan masyarakat saat ini, sembari membangun bisnis rendah karbon yang dapat mendukung kemandirian energi Indonesia di masa depan.

“Untuk memenuhi kebutuhan kita, energi yang existing tetap dijalankan, sembari terus mengembangkan energi yang ramah lingkungan,” pungkas Arya.

text:
An unnamed energy company plans to work with Chinese pyrolysis technology provider Niutech on a refinery upgrade to turn waste plastic into material for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), potentially helping to tackle rising plastic waste and the aviation industry's push for cleaner fuel.

Under a new deal, an unnamed energy company will work with Chinese pyrolysis technology provider Niutech to install an industrial-scale unit that turns waste plastic into material for sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF.

Here's what to know

According to Interesting Engineering, the plan is to add the system to an existing refinery, linking plastic-waste treatment with hydrotreated SAF production so that discarded plastic can move through a single chain into jet-fuel ingredients.

Niutech's system uses continuous pyrolysis, heating plastic with limited oxygen so it breaks down into hydrocarbon products such as pyrolysis oil. That oil can then be further refined into SAF. The planned production line will have a single-unit capacity of about 11,023 to 55,116 US tons per year (10,000 to 50,000 metric tons per year).

One notable aspect of the system is the range of plastics Niutech said it can process. The company said it can handle plastics such as polypropylene, polyethylene, polystyrene, acrylonitrile butadiene styrene, and nylon, either individually or in mixed streams.

Mixed and contaminated plastic waste is often difficult and expensive to recycle. If a commercial system can avoid extensive washing, sorting, and drying, it could lower processing costs and make it easier to handle plastic that might otherwise end up in landfills, incinerators, or nearby communities as pollution.

More background

The agreement comes as airlines and fuel producers race to expand SAF supply. Under the EU's ReFuelEU Aviation rules, SAF must account for 2% of fuel supplied at EU airports in 2025, rising to 6% in 2030 and 70% by 2050.

Used cooking oil and similar waste oils are established SAF feedstocks, but supply remains constrained. Waste plastic could offer another source of hydrocarbons, particularly for facilities already equipped to refine fuel at scale.

Better systems for handling low-value plastic waste could ease pressure on local waste streams, reduce pollution risks, and support cleaner air by displacing some fossil-based inputs in aviation fuel production.

Niutech also said it has deployed continuous pyrolysis systems in the United Kingdom, South Korea, Denmark, Thailand, Vietnam, and China, with multiple projects already delivering roughly 11,023 US tons per year (10,000 metric tons per year).

What's being done?

The agreement is aimed at integrating the technology into a refinery setting rather than treating plastic-to-fuel as a small pilot project, where continuous operation is essential to both output and economics.

If successful, the project could open a larger commercial market for harder-to-recycle plastics while giving fuel producers another way to meet SAF targets. In practical terms, that could help diversify supply and potentially ease some of the cost pressure tied to limited feedstocks.

Still, it is not a replacement for reducing unnecessary plastic use in the first place. Households can continue cutting waste and saving money by choosing reusable goods and choosing plastic-free options for everyday products when possible.

The next major test will be whether waste plastic-to-SAF systems can run reliably, make economic sense, and perform at industrial scale. If they can, this refinery upgrade could point to a future in which more discarded plastic is put to use instead of piling up as pollution.

Where can I learn more?

This refinery plan is part of a broader push to find better uses for plastic that conventional recycling often can't handle. Other reporting and research in this space follow new fuel pathways, emerging chemical processes, and the bigger question of what to do with low-value waste that keeps piling up.

• Scientists have shown that powerful clean fuel from plastic waste could help power hydrogen cars.

• At Virginia Tech, engineers are advancing breakthroughs that could revolutionize how plastic gets reused.

• At the University of Texas, lasers may permanently change plastic by recovering reusable chemicals.

• Greenpeace argues plastic recycling is a failed concept as U.S. waste keeps rising.

That wider backdrop helps explain why plastic-to-SAF is getting attention as traditional recycling continues to fall short. It also highlights the big question behind all of these efforts: whether newer conversion technologies can move beyond the lab and work at commercial scale.

text:
Randall Stuewe, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Darling Ingredients Inc DAR, sold 5,000 shares of the company's stock on September 2, 2026, according to a recent SEC Filing. Following the transaction, the insider now directly owns 1,133,467 shares of the company.

The sale was executed at a price of $68.20 per share, representing a transaction value of approximately $341,000. This insider sale comes at a time when the stock is trading at levels that GuruFocus valuation metrics suggest are significantly above the company's intrinsic worth.

Insider Trading Activity and Trends

Over the past year, Randall Stuewe has been a net seller of Darling Ingredients stock. The insider has sold a total of 35,000 shares during this period while purchasing 0 shares. This latest transaction continues a pattern of consistent selling by the company's top executive.

The broader insider trading picture for Darling Ingredients reveals a notable imbalance between buying and selling activity. Over the past year, there has been only 1 insider buy transaction recorded for the company. In contrast, there have been 11 insider sell transactions during the same timeframe. This significant disparity between buying and selling activity among company insiders often warrants attention from investors, as insiders typically have the most intimate knowledge of their company's operations, prospects, and valuation.

While insider selling can occur for a variety of personal financial reasons—such as portfolio diversification, tax planning, or funding personal expenses—the consistent pattern of selling by the Chairman and CEO, combined with the limited buying activity from other insiders, may suggest that those closest to the company believe the current share price does not offer an attractive entry point.

Company Overview

Darling Ingredients Inc is a global leader in the production of natural ingredients from edible and inedible bio-nutrients. The company operates through three primary business segments: Feed Ingredients, Food Ingredients, and Fuel Ingredients. Darling collects and transforms animal by-products and food waste into a wide range of products including fats, proteins, and other specialty ingredients used in animal feed, human food, pharmaceuticals, and renewable fuels.

The company's operations span across North America, Europe, South America, and Asia, serving customers in the agricultural, food processing, and energy sectors. Darling Ingredients has positioned itself as a key player in the circular economy, converting what would otherwise be waste streams into valuable products. The company's Fuel Ingredients segment, which produces renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel through its Diamond Green Diesel joint venture, has become an increasingly important growth driver as global demand for low-carbon transportation fuels continues to rise.

Valuation Analysis

Shares of Darling Ingredients were trading at $68.20 on the day of Randall Stuewe's recent sale. This price gives the stock a market cap of approximately $10.29 billion.

From a valuation perspective, the stock trades at a price-earnings ratio of 17.57, which is higher than the industry median of 15.93. However, this figure is lower than the company's own historical median price-earnings ratio, suggesting that the stock may be trading at a more reasonable earnings multiple than it has in the past.

GuruFocus's proprietary GF Value metric provides additional context for evaluating the stock's current valuation. The GF Value is an intrinsic-value estimate calculated from three primary factors: historical trading multiples (including price-earnings ratio, price-sales ratio, price-book ratio, and price-to-free cash flow), a GuruFocus adjustment factor based on the company's past returns and growth, and future estimates of business performance from Morningstar analysts.

Based on this comprehensive valuation methodology, Darling Ingredients has a GuruFocus Value of $42.36 per share. With the stock trading at $68.20, the price-to-GF-Value ratio stands at 1.61. This indicates that the stock is Significantly Overvalued according to GuruFocus's assessment. In other words, investors are currently paying approximately 61% more than the estimated intrinsic value of the company based on historical valuation metrics, past performance, and analyst projections.

The combination of insider selling activity and the stock's significant overvaluation relative to its GF Value may suggest that the current share price has outpaced the company's fundamental value. For value-oriented investors, this could indicate that patience might be rewarded, as the stock may eventually revert to a more reasonable valuation level.

Guru Ownership and Institutional Activity

Beyond insider activity, GuruFocus tracks the 13F filings of prominent investment gurus to provide insight into how the world's most successful investors are positioning themselves in various stocks. This premium data is a differentiator for GuruFocus and is not available on other financial platforms such as Simply Wall St or Morningstar.

Currently, 13 gurus hold shares of Darling Ingredients Inc, with 6 adding to their positions and 7 trimming their holdings in recent quarters. This relatively balanced split between buyers and sellers among prominent investors suggests a degree of uncertainty regarding the stock's near-term prospects. While some gurus see value in the company's long-term growth potential—particularly in the renewable fuels space—others appear to be taking profits or reducing exposure at current valuation levels.

The fact that more gurus are trimming than adding, combined with the insider selling activity, creates a picture of cautious sentiment among sophisticated market participants. However, it is worth noting that the 6 gurus who added to their positions during this period demonstrate that there remains conviction in the company's fundamental story and future growth opportunities.

Conclusion

The recent insider sale by Chairman and CEO Randall Stuewe adds to a pattern of consistent selling over the past year. While insider transactions should never be viewed in isolation, the combination of ongoing insider selling, limited insider buying, and a stock price that GuruFocus considers significantly overvalued relative to its GF Value may give investors reason for pause.

Darling Ingredients operates in attractive end markets with growing demand for sustainable ingredients and renewable fuels. However, at $68.20 per share, investors are paying a substantial premium to the company's estimated intrinsic value of $42.36. The insider activity and valuation metrics together suggest that the current share price may already reflect much of the company's positive outlook, leaving limited margin of safety for new investors.

As always, investors should conduct their own thorough research and consider their individual investment objectives and risk tolerance before making any investment decisions based on insider activity or valuation metrics.

text:
A global manufacturer of agricultural machinery is expanding its harvesting portfolio to include new headers, tedders, intelligent automation systems and precision technologies.

CLAAS of America’s new offering ranges from forage and grain harvesting to hay tools, designed to help producers maximize throughput, improve crop quality and make more informed decisions about their entire operation.

"Innovation starts with listening to our customers," said Dennis Ogle, head of sales for self-propelled harvesters.

"Every product we're introducing reflects our commitment to North American producers and the way they farm, bringing together advanced technology, proven performance and practical solutions that help them operate more efficiently every day."

Expanding forage harvesting efficiency

CLAAS continues to expand its JAGUAR forage harvesting portfolio with new headers and intelligent automation designed to maximize throughput, improve crop quality and help operators get the most from every harvesting window.

The ORBIS 12000 is a new 16-row corn header engineered specifically for CLAAS JAGUAR 1000 series forage harvester. Designed to keep the industry's highest-capacity forage harvester operating at peak productivity, the ORBIS 12000 delivers smooth crop flow, exceptional throughput and the flexibility to perform across a wide range of crop conditions.

Also joining the JAGUAR 1000 series lineup is the DD 8400 Direct Disc header, featuring a 27.5-foot working width for efficient whole-crop harvesting. The header delivers excellent ground following and consistent crop flow to deliver clean cutting performance while maximizing forage quality and machine productivity.

CLAAS is also introducing CEMOS AUTO KNIFE CONDITION, an intelligent automation system that continuously monitors harvesting conditions and determines the optimal time and number of sharpening passes needed to maintain peak knife performance. By automating the sharpening process, the system helps reduce knife wear and fuel consumption while maintaining consistent chop quality and maximizing harvesting capacity. The result is greater productivity and more consistent performance throughout the harvest season, regardless of operator experience.

Added intelligence for combine harvesting

New CLAAS combine harvesting accessories, and precision technologies have been designed to help producers maximize throughput, protect grain quality and make more informed decisions.

Leading the lineup is the ROVIO 5 Series, a corn head designed and manufactured exclusively by CLAAS. Engineered to integrate seamlessly with LEXION and TRION combines, it features a redesigned picking system, larger intake auger and integrated horizontal choppers that deliver smoother crop flow, increased throughput and cleaner residue management across a wide range of harvest conditions. The head is offered in 12-, 16-, and 18-row models with 30 in. row spacing.

READ NEXT: CORN SILAGE HARVEST: TIMING, PACKING REQUIREMENTS FOR MAXIMUM BUTRIENT RETENTION

To complement to the ROVIO 5 head, both CLAAS combine lines in 2027 offer an electronic machine optimization system designed exclusively for corn crops. CEMOS Corn continuously optimizes combine performance as conditions change throughout the day. The intelligent automation system automatically adjusts machine settings for corn to help maximize grain quality, minimize grain loss and maintain peak harvesting efficiency, allowing operators to spend less time making manual adjustments and more time focused on the harvest.

Once the grain has entered the machine, the new NUTRIMETER GRAIN system--available on LEXION series combines--provides operators with real-time insights using advanced transmissive near-infrared (NIR) technology. Without stopping the combine, operators can continuously measure moisture, protein and other key crop characteristics. The information is automatically captured within CLAAS connect, providing valuable harvest data that supports grain marketing, crop management and future agronomic decisions.

Hay and forage innovation

CLAAS is also expanding the middle range of its hay and forage implement offering with three new VOLTO T series tedders with working widths ranging from 25 feet 3 inches to 35 feet 5 inches and the proven MAX SPREAD crop concept, engineered to deliver faster, more uniform crop drying through gentle crop handling, excellent ground following and high-output performance. The latest model offering includes the 25-foot, 3-inch VOLTO 800 TH, the 28-foot, 6-inch VOLTO 900 T, and 35-foot, 5-inch VOLTO 1100 T.

The latest models offer a new power train with hermetically sealed rotor gearboxes, a new rotor wheel mounting with a reinforced rotor shaft and new spreading angle adjustment for angles of up to 18 degrees. The range boasts reduced hydraulic requirements, KENNFIXX couplings for all hydraulic connections and PERMALINK HD finger clutches passed down from larger models.

By helping producers preserve forage quality while improving field efficiency, the latest VOLTO models complement the company's growing lineup of harvesting solutions designed to maximize throughput, crop quality and overall productivity from the first cut through harvest.

These new harvesting technologies complement the next generation of CLAAS equipment, reflecting the company's continued investment in helping producers meet the growing demands of modern agriculture.

"Every product we've introduced was engineered with one purpose in mind: helping our customers do more," Ogle said.

"More acres in a day. More confidence in every decision. More value from every harvest. That's what made for more means, and that's the standard we're committed to delivering."

text:
Biomanufacturing uses biological systems to produce chemicals or materials. For example, scientists use microbes’ ability to ferment alcohol to develop bio-based fuels. In advanced aviation fuels, new formulas could have better performance and efficiency than current ones. One potential high-performance bio-based jet fuel is made from a chemical that is difficult to produce. However, biomanufacturing has the potential to make a precursor to this chemical, isoprenol. Scientists have tested production pathways in many microbial systems. However, we still need microbial hosts that can produce industrially relevant amounts of this chemical. Researchers tested producing isoprenol in a type of yeast.

The Impact

The yeast the researchers tested has a natural ability to accumulate oil, among other unique characteristics. They engineered a production pathway into the yeast and demonstrated that it could produce isoprenol. They also tested modifications to the pathway and explored solutions to bottlenecks in production. These findings show that this yeast is a possible host for isoprenol production. It provides a foundation for future research on biomanufacturing isoprenol. Potentially, it could help meet the demand for domestically produced aviation fuels.

Summary

Biomanufacturing of isoprenol has been achieved through a metabolic pathway known as the IPP-bypass pathway. But many microbial hosts have struggled with producing isoprenol in a biomanufacturing setting. There is a need for microbial hosts that are compatible with biomanufacturing and can produce industrially relevant titers of isoprenol. Researchers at the Joint BioEnergy Institute sought to investigate isoprenol production in Rhodosporidium toruloides. This is a type of oil-accumulating yeast that is a promising microbial host for biomanufacturing. They implemented the IPP-bypass pathway into R. toruloides and achieved production of isoprenol up to 93.1 mg/L in a sugar-rich medium and 27.3 mg/L using a sorghum-derived feedstock. They identified engineering methods that could improve isoprenol production in future research. Overall, this work provides an initial understanding of isoprenol production in R. toruloides and provides guidance for future research efforts.

text:
It is sometimes said that in Washington, a bad idea never dies. This may illuminate why the leader of a DC-based interest group recently penned an opinion editorial that yet again sought a policy audience to disparage our industry, this time in connection with this summer’s FIFA World Cup games.

The biased op-ed published in The Hill, a congressionally focused outlet, selectively used flight data to U.S. cities that hosted World Cup games to denounce business aviation’s sustainability record; more broadly, the piece left readers in the dark about our industry’s value to citizens, companies and communities.

We could not let it go unanswered.

When business aviation is maligned this way – in the media, on Capitol Hill or elsewhere – NBAA fiercely defends it, standing strong and setting the record straight. My published response in The Hill provided a fact check highlighting critical information the op-ed’s author overlooked or omitted from his piece.

Take, for example, the op-ed’s mischaracterizations about business aviation and sustainability. As my response pointed out, experts have long acknowledged that our sector has always amounted to a tiny fraction of transportation emissions. We have particularly made progress in the past four decades – slashing business aviation’s carbon footprint by 40%, with breakthroughs including lightweight composites, winglets, cleaner, quieter engines and other technologies.

title: JAL Acquires Hanjin KAL Stake, Forging Comprehensive Alliance with Korean Air

text:
Japan Airlines (JAL) has acquired a stake in Hanjin KAL, the holding company of Korean Air, joining as an ally of Hanjin Group Chairman Cho Won-tae. While the stake size and acquisition amount were not disclosed, expectations are growing that this investment could serve as a white knight role, given that it comes at a time when the possibility of a management control dispute with Hoban Group is intensifying.

According to the aviation industry on the 4th, JAL announced the previous day in Tokyo that it had acquired Hanjin KAL shares while signing a strategic partnership with Korean Air. Korean Air explained that "JAL independently decided to invest after considering Hanjin KAL's long-term market value." It was reported that no large shareholding disclosure — required for stakes of 5% or more — has been filed.

The investment comes as Hoban Group has been rapidly expanding its stake in Hanjin KAL, narrowing the gap with Chairman Cho's camp. Hoban Group raised its Hanjin KAL stake to 20.15% in July. Based on the semi-annual report, Chairman Cho and his related parties held 20.57%, meaning the gap was a mere 0.42 percentage points.

If JAL's acquired stake is classified as friendly to Chairman Cho's camp, it would provide significant support for defending management control. Looking at Hanjin KAL's current major shareholder structure, Delta Air Lines holds 14.90%, the Korea Development Bank holds 10.58%, and the National Pension Service holds 5.11%. Among these, Delta Air Lines and the Korea Development Bank are classified as friendly to Chairman Cho's camp. With JAL's stake added, Chairman Cho's camp would hold well over 46%, overwhelming Hoban Group's position.

JAL's emergence is particularly significant given the possibility that the Korea Development Bank may sell its stake. There are observations that the state-run bank could divest its 10.58% holding to recover public funds following the integration of Korean Air and Asiana Airlines. Concerns have been raised that if the Korea Development Bank — which played a white knight role during the 2019 management dispute between Chairman Cho and his sister, former Vice President Cho Hyun-ah — were to sell its stake, a full-scale dispute with Hoban Group could erupt.

Chairman Cho has a track record of bringing in foreign airlines as allies through business cooperation. During the 2019 dispute with a three-party coalition, Delta Air Lines acquired a stake in Hanjin KAL, lending support to Chairman Cho's camp. Delta has since continued to expand its cooperation with Korean Air, including pursuing a joint acquisition of Canada's WestJet.

The strategic partnership with JAL extends beyond a simple equity investment to encompass the entire business spectrum. Despite belonging to different global airline alliances — Korean Air is a member of SkyTeam while JAL belongs to oneworld — the two carriers have decided to build an individual cooperative relationship that transcends these affiliations.

Passenger operations will see the first wave of enhanced cooperation. Korean Air has applied codesharing to all Korea-Japan routes since 2014, and with the upcoming merger with Asiana Airlines in December, Asiana's Korea-Japan routes will also be included in the joint operation. Korean Air's Japan routes, currently at around 250 weekly flights, are expected to expand to approximately 400 flights after integration.

Cargo operations will also see broadened cooperation. The two airlines have agreed to jointly utilize cargo terminals they have established around the world. Shared terminal usage can simultaneously deliver two benefits: expansion of the global sales network and reduction of fixed logistics costs. Personnel exchanges will also begin to address airport ground handling staff shortages. The carriers plan to activate human resource exchanges, including mutual use of crew training facilities.

The two airlines will form a task force to explore new business cooperation models. Starting with aircraft maintenance, repair, and overhaul (MRO), they plan to concretize cooperation in future businesses including the expanded adoption of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) for carbon neutrality and urban air mobility (UAM). They will also pursue joint investments in startups to secure source technologies for new businesses.

The cooperative history between Korean Air and JAL spans well over 60 years. The two carriers began collaborating in 1963, two years before diplomatic normalization between South Korea and Japan. At that time, Korean Air Lines Corporation — Korean Air's predecessor — and JAL signed an "Agreement on the Basic Concept of Bilateral Alliance." At a time when intergovernmental agreements were difficult to conclude, the two airlines first created a framework for agreement and obtained approval from both governments, playing a role in opening the door to Korea-Japan diplomatic normalization.

The following year, in 1964, Korea-Japan routes were established. Korean Air opened the Seoul–Osaka route, while JAL opened the Seoul–Tokyo route. In 1967, the Busan–Fukuoka route was added, laying the foundation for expanded exchanges between the two countries. Since 2004, the carriers have applied their own codesharing to broaden cooperation, and since 2016, they have operated an alliance program allowing Korean Air customers to earn Korean Air miles when flying on JAL aircraft.

Choi Jeong-ho, Korean Air's Executive Vice President, said, "Through this strategic partnership, we will be able to combine the outstanding infrastructure and know-how possessed by both companies to maximize customer benefits. Going forward, we will continue to strengthen our competitiveness in the aviation market and provide the best possible service to passengers through close cooperation with global partners."

With this cooperation, Korean Air has further strengthened its global network competitiveness ahead of its integration with Asiana Airlines. JAL has likewise secured an opportunity to solidify its position on Korea-Japan routes while realizing economies of scale in cargo, maintenance, and new business areas. Amid a trend of expanding individual alliances between airlines in the global aviation industry, attention is focused on whether this cross-border cooperation model between two carriers belonging to different alliance groups will set a precedent for future industry restructuring.

text:
Japan Airlines has acquired a stake in Hanjin KAL, the holding company of Korean Air, in a move that supports the view that the Japanese carrier has joined as a white knight for Hanjin KAL Chairman Cho Won-tae, whose control is under threat from second-largest shareholder Hoban Group. JAL elevated its relationship with Korean Air to that of a strategic partner.

Korean Air (003490) and JAL are also moving to strengthen their position in the global aviation industry. Building on more than 60 years of cooperation, the two carriers agreed to expand Korea-Japan codeshare flights to 400 a week from the December launch of the merged Korean Air. Korean Air will also work closely with JAL on new businesses including aircraft maintenance, the adoption of sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, and urban air mobility, or UAM.

Stake Purchase Comes Amid Control Dispute

According to the aviation industry and the Nihon Keizai Shimbun on the 4th, JAL signed a strategic partnership with Korean Air and acquired a portion of Hanjin KAL shares. The size of the stake and the purchase price were not disclosed.

JAL is expected to serve as an ally to Cho, much as Delta Air Lines of the United States does with its 14.90% stake in Hanjin KAL. Hoban Group recently raised its Hanjin KAL holding to 20.15%, narrowing the gap with Cho to 0.41 percentage point.

Concerns have surfaced that the Korea Development Bank could sell its 10.58% stake to recover public funds following the merger of Korean Air and Asiana Airlines (020560). The state lender has acted as a white knight since a family dispute over management control erupted in 2019, and its exit could trigger a full-blown fight with Hoban Group.

Cho is seen as having drawn JAL into his camp through business cooperation to dispel such concerns. He also brought in Delta Air Lines as an ally in 2019, when he was locked in a dispute with a three-way alliance that included his sister, former Korean Air Vice President Cho Hyun-ah. Delta, which holds 14.90% of Hanjin KAL, has been widening its cooperation with Korean Air, including a joint bid for Canadian carrier WestJet.

Korea-Japan Codeshare to Expand to 400 Flights After Asiana Merger

Korean Air and JAL, the flagship carriers of Korea and Japan, declared on the 3rd in Tokyo that they would enter a strategic partnership. Korean Air belongs to SkyTeam and JAL to Oneworld, but the two agreed to build a bilateral alliance that goes beyond those groupings.

The two carriers will first strengthen cooperation in their core passenger and cargo businesses. Korean Air has applied codesharing with JAL on all routes between Korea and Japan since 2014, and the Japan routes of Asiana Airlines, which will be merged in December, will also be included. Korean Air currently operates about 250 flights a week on Japan routes, a figure expected to rise to about 400 after the merger with Asiana.

Cooperation in the cargo business will also deepen. Korean Air and JAL have moved toward jointly using the cargo terminals the two have built around the world. Sharing cargo terminals expands their global sales networks and can sharply reduce fixed costs such as logistics expenses. To address airport labor shortages, the two will also step up personnel exchanges, starting with ground handling and extending to mutual use of cabin crew training facilities.

Korean Air and JAL will also form a task force to pursue new businesses. The task force will design new cooperation models starting with aircraft maintenance, repair and overhaul, or MRO, and extending to expanded SAF use for carbon neutrality and to UAM and other future businesses. The two will also seek to secure core technologies in new business areas through joint investments in startups.

Cooperation between Korean Air and JAL dates back more than 60 years. The two carriers began working together in 1963, two years before Korea and Japan normalized diplomatic relations in 1965. At the time, Korean Air Lines Corporation, the predecessor of Korean Air, and JAL signed an agreement on the basic framework of their partnership. With a government-to-government accord difficult at the time, the two airlines first built a framework and then won approval from both governments, helping open the way for the normalization of relations.

The alliance blueprint the two carriers drew up ahead of their governments led to the opening of Korea-Japan routes the following year. Korean Air opened a Seoul-Osaka route and JAL a Seoul-Tokyo route. A Busan-Fukuoka route followed in 1967, providing a stepping stone for active exchanges between the political and business circles of the two countries.

Although they belong to different global airline alliances, Korean Air and JAL have widened their cooperation, including their own codeshare arrangement introduced in 2004. Codesharing allows a carrier to sell tickets on a partner's flight under its own flight number, expanding route networks while offering passengers more convenient booking. Since 2016, the two have also run a program that lets Korean Air customers earn Korean Air mileage when flying on JAL aircraft.

"Through this strategic partnership, the two companies will be able to maximize customer benefits by combining their outstanding infrastructure and know-how," said Choi Jung-ho, vice president of Korean Air. "We will continue to strengthen our competitiveness in the aviation market through close cooperation with global partners and provide the best service to passengers."

text:
The leading aviation industry conference in the Baltic region, the Riga Aviation Forum, will bring together top-level aviation leaders, policymakers, experts, and business executives from the Baltics, the Nordics, and across Europe on 10 September 2026 at Hanzas Perons in Riga. Participants will discuss the future of aviation and related industries, and their role in driving regional economic growth, strengthening connectivity, and fostering manufacturing and innovation.

Organized by the Latvian Aviation Association in cooperation with its partners, the Riga Aviation Forum is celebrating its milestone anniversary this year. Over the past ten years, it has become the foremost meeting place for aviation decision-makers in the Baltic region and the leading platform for strategic dialogue between the aviation industry, government institutions, tourism stakeholders, and international organizations.

The 2026 Riga Aviation Forum programme, which will be opened by Minister of Transport of Latvia Rihards Kozlovskis, reflects the most pressing trends and challenges shaping aviation development regionally and globally. The Forum’s keynote discussion, moderated by Raimonds Gruntiņš, Regional Director Europe at the International Air Transport Association (IATA), will feature Sanders Salmu, Deputy Secretary General of the Estonian Ministry of Climate; Elīna Šimiņa-Neverovska, Deputy State Secretary at Latvia’s Ministry of Transport; Erno Hildén, CEO and President of Latvia’s national airline airBaltic and experienced industry professional from Lithuania Gediminas Almantas. The discussion will focus on aviation policymaking at the national, regional, and European levels.

Another major topic of the Forum will be the importance of collaboration between government institutions, tourism organizations, and aviation industry stakeholders in driving economic growth. Participants in this session will include Laila Odiņa, CEO of RIX Riga Airport; Ieva Jāgere, Director of the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA); Olga Gončarova, Head of Lithuania Travel; and Mari Saloniemi, representative of Visit Tampere.

The pressing challenge of workforce development and talent attraction will be examined by leading industry experts, including international aviation specialist Jane Hoskisson, Iluta Savicka, Head of Norwegian’s Riga Base, Aivars Pūcītis, Board Member of Latvijas Gaisa Satiksme, and other experienced HR and talent management professionals.

A further key topic, the transition from traditional infrastructure development to integrated and intelligent aviation ecosystems in the development of Baltic airports, will be explored in depth by industry experts representing SITA, one of the world’s leading air transport communications and information technology companies, as well as executives from Latvijas Gaisa Satiksme and Lithuania’s aviation industry association CAVIA.

A dedicated Forum session will focus on businesses operating “behind the runway” - sectors closely linked to aviation that are playing an increasingly important role in industry growth as airports evolve into new forms of urban environments. Leading experts including Walter Seib, Chairman of Avolta; Borga Dincler, Business Development and Marketing Director at Turkish airport advertising operator Media Port; Aude Ferrand, Chairwoman of TAV Operation Services and Chief Commercial Officer of TAV Airports; and other distinguished speakers will share their vision for innovative services and future passenger experiences in airport cities of tomorrow.

The Forum will also address the critical topic of manufacturing and supply chains, their resilience, and their ability to adapt to sustainability challenges and rapid industry transformation. Insights will be provided by experts including Jānis Kisiels, CEO of sustainable aviation fuel producer NorSAF; Gytis Leonavicius, CEO of Lithuania’s Skyco; as well as leaders from companies AM Craft, Axon Cable, and Artex Latvia.

In addition to the conference programme, RAF 2026 will offer extensive networking opportunities for aviation professionals, business leaders, public sector representatives, investors, and representatives of international organizations from across Europe.

Further information and the full programme are available at RAF website.

text:
In light of the digitalization of European rail freight transport, PJM has developed the WaggonTracker system, which provides central digital train functions. According to PJM, several thousand of these systems are already in use internationally, including by companies such as SBB Cargo, FS LogistiX, Mercer, Plasser & Theurer, TRANSWAGGON, VTG, and Tatravagónka. The company will also present its latest developments at Innotrans, which takes place from September 22 to 25, 2026.

Functionalities of the WaggonTracker System

The WaggonTracker integrates digital train functions, real-time monitoring, and an autonomous power supply ensured by axle bearing generators. A standout feature of the system is the Automatic Brake Test, which has been in practical use since 2017. This technology is considered the only approved system worldwide that significantly accelerates train preparation.

As part of the DAC4EU project, the technology has also proven itself in DAK test trains of the Westfälische Landes-Eisenbahn (WLE). The WaggonTracker already fulfills essential functions that meet the upcoming European standards for the Digital Automatic Coupler (DAK). These include power and data supply, determination of train composition, train length, and train integrity, as well as the automated brake test.

Modular Design and Integration

The system is characterized by a modular design that allows for flexible integration into new and existing wagons from various manufacturers. This flexibility offers both efficiency and safety advantages and creates a solid foundation for the ongoing digitalization and rollout of the DAK in European rail freight transport. PJM thus positions itself as a provider that actively addresses the challenges of digitalization in rail freight transport and offers solutions that meet the industry’s requirements.

text:
Calumet Inc. subsidiary Montana Renewables LLC has revised its previously announced sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) expansion, or MaxSAF project, at the operator’s renewable fuels manufacturing plant in Great Falls, Mont.

Montana Renewables now estimates remaining expansion capital at $137 million, compared with about $1.2 billion contemplated under the original Phase 2 project, Calumet said in a release Sept. 1.

The revised plan proposes repurposing and redeployment of existing equipment from the adjacent Calumet Montana Refining (CMR) asphalt plant that will be transferred to Montana Renewables under a long-term lease.

Specific assets planned for repurposing and transfer from CMR include a hydrotreater, hydrogen plant, and naphtha splitter. The tied-in hydrotreater ultimately will create a proprietary dual-reactor configuration at the renewable fuels plant, according to Calumet.

The second reactor will operate in a “polishing” service rather than the conventional “cracking” service to achieve a configuration aimed at improving SAF yields, reducing by-product formation, and limiting yield loss.

Additional modular equipment, including a third renewable fuels reactor currently located offsite, could support capacity increases beyond 200 million gal/year, Calumet said.

The revised program consists of six discrete projects rather than one large construction effort, with each project designed to remove specific operating constraints and enable a shorter payback period.

Montana Renewables currently produces SAF at an estimated rate of 60 million gal/year rfollowing constraint-removal work completed during a spring 2026 turnaround, according to Calumet.

In the near-term and following the proposed expansion, the parent company said it expects SAF production at Montana Renewables’ plant to:

Exceed an 80-million gal/year rate by yearend 2026.

Surpass 120 million gal/year by spring 2027.

Reach about 200 million gal/year by yearend 2028.

The expansion also will result in recovery of about 20 million gal/year of renewable propane and butane previously used as fuel gas. The plan includes improved renewable naphtha yields and lower unit operating costs via higher throughput and reduced water consumption, Calumet said.

Feedstock consumption at the renewable fuels plant will reach about 2 billion lb/year of ranch- and farm-originated materials used to produce renewable jet fuel, diesel, and gasoline.

While equipment tie-ins as part of the expansion are scheduled to be completed during a fourth-quarter 2026 turnaround, Calumet said CMR will continue producing retail asphalt and retain its employees. Post-expansion, CMR and Montana Renewables also will share unidentified site infrastructure and other costs.

Announced in 2023, the original MaxSAF plan called for increasing Great Falls SAF production by more than 700% to about 300 million gal/year. Combined SAF and renewable diesel capacity at the time was anticipated to reach about 330 million gal/year.

The original project also included a second renewable fuels reactor, debottlenecking of renewable fuels and feedstock pretreatment units, SAF blending and logistics equipment, expanded renewable hydrogen production, cogeneration, and water treatment and recycling systems.

Financing and loan revision

The revised MaxSAF project follows an amendment to the loan guarantee agreement between Montana Renewables and the US Department of Energy (DOE) originally executed in January 2025.

The DOE’s Phase 2 funding commitment has been reduced to a single final draw of $34 million from up to $658 million in the original agreement. Calumet said Montana Renewables expects to fund the balance of the revised expansion through retained earnings.

The amended structure does not require third-party equity, which Calumet said eliminates additional dilution while maintaining a simpler capital structure.

Funded in February 2025, the first DOE tranche totaling $782 million recapitalized Montana Renewables and supported eligible previously incurred expenses. Calumet also made a $150 million equity investment using cash on hand.

Under the now-amended agreement, the final $34 million draw remains subject to commercial, technical, and legal conditions. During construction, Calumet said it expected retained earnings to supplement DOE funds and keep debt below 55% of eligible project spending.

The loan retains its 15-year tenor and annual interest rate of the US Treasury rate plus 3/8%. Principal and interest payments remain deferred until MaxSAF is commissioned.

The first debt-service date remains March 2029, with maturity in December 2039.

title: Corn demand needed: Michigan's case for becoming a sustainable aviation fuel hub
description:
Hosted by the Corn Marketing Program of Michigan and partners, the event in Dearborn brought together ag and industry leaders to focus on positioning Michigan as a leader in sustainable fuel production, including sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).
For farmers, the importance of sustainable fuel production boils down to demand.
As a new report commissioned by Michigan Corn states, “Michigan’s existing corn and ethanol economy is well-positioned” to develop an ethanol-to-jet hub, presenting a sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) market opportunity for the state’s growers and transportation industry.
The report makes the case for an SAF production hub and supporting campus in Southeast Michigan, where Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport and the Port of Detroit sit within a single logistics footprint.
READ NEXT: WHAT'S THE FUTURE OF SUSTAINABLE AVIATION FUEL?
text:
How do you keep farmers farming?

The key will be finding new markets — and nothing matches the size and scalability of the biofuel market, according to experts who spoke at this week’s Great Lakes Sustainable Fuels Symposium.

Hosted by the Corn Marketing Program of Michigan and partners, the event in Dearborn brought together ag and industry leaders to focus on positioning Michigan as a leader in sustainable fuel production, including sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

For farmers, the importance of sustainable fuel production boils down to demand.

“Nearly 100 years ago, we produced about 2 billion bushels of corn across 106 million acres,” said Matt Frostic, a Sanilac County Farm Bureau member who will take over as president of the National Corn Growers Association (NCGA) in less than a month.

“Today, we produce about 17 billion bushels on about 90 million acres, give or take.”

It’s a lot of bushels that came with a lot of financial losses. NCGA estimated a loss of $0.93 per bushel for corn growers across the U.S. last year.

While there used to be talk of how farmers would have to meet demand to feed the world decades from now, that’s not the story anymore, S&P Global Head of Agribusiness Accounting Juan Sacoto said during the symposium.

The story now, he said, is how to keep farmers going.

“I think the U.S. is the epicenter of this, but it is a global problem,” Sacoto said.

“If we do nothing, if we let the world go just as it is now, there's great probability that essentially we have to let some acreage go down,” he later added. Sacoto painted a bleak picture of how falling prices drag down profitability, then investment and innovation, before acreage declines with it.

The case for SAF

So, how can Michigan help keep that decline from happening? The answer could be found in the skies.

As a new report commissioned by Michigan Corn states, “Michigan’s existing corn and ethanol economy is well-positioned” to develop an ethanol-to-jet hub, presenting a sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) market opportunity for the state’s growers and transportation industry.

The report makes the case for an SAF production hub and supporting campus in Southeast Michigan, where Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport and the Port of Detroit sit within a single logistics footprint.

“No other location combines feedstock access, an international air gateway with an onsite refueling market, and deepwater export capacity within a 30-mile radius,” the report adds.

As the report also notes, Michigan already has systems to verify the implementation of on-farm conservation practices, with models available to estimate carbon-intensity scores for farms with verified practices. It cites thousands of farms that have already been verified under the Michigan Agriculture Environmental Assurance Program (MAEAP).

While adding incentives to SAF and biofuel production at the state level has been used in hopes of bolstering production in places like Minnesota, Delta Airlines Senior Manager of SAF Commercial Strategy Yvonne Domeier said airlines look at SAF from an economic perspective.

“It's supply and ultimately cost, and it's important to understand that SAF today is anywhere from two to five times more expensive than conventional jet fuel,” Domeier said before joining representatives from Growth Energy, the nation’ largest biofuels trade organization, and the executive director of the Detroit Port Authority for a panel discussion.

“From an airline perspective, how we would continue to take delivery of more staff is really going to be financially driven,” she continued, noting that incentives at the state level need to be supportive of the entire value chain — including farmers.

Domeier’s advice for farmers and renewable fuel advocates is to make their voices heard.

“Make sure that our legislators know how important the ag community is to biofuels, to sustainable aviation fuel, and that all parties need to see the value in that from a financial perspective in order for us to unlock those new markets and drive the biofuel industry,” she said.

READ NEXT: WHAT'S THE FUTURE OF SUSTAINABLE AVIATION FUEL? HERE'S A REALISTIC LOOK…

State incentives proposed

While Michigan isn’t currently producing SAF right now, Michigan House bills 4424 and 4425 aim to change that by creating tax incentives to jumpstart production.

The bills would provide a $1.50 per gallon tax credit for SAF purchasers, producers, or blenders, while capping incentives at $4.5 million in year one and $9 million annually thereafter.

It all adds up to supporting the production of ethanol-derived aviation fuels, said Michigan Farm Bureau Associate Legislative Counsel Josh Scramlin, who noted that the bills put an emphasis on Michigan-grown feedstocks.

"Michigan is the ideal place to produce SAF, because not only are we a large corn producing state, but we have DTW, which is one of the busiest airports in the country,” Scramlin added.

“We have the crops, and we have the air traffic.”

Canadian canola crushers set a record in the crop year just ended, and the industry celebrated the achievement of an ever-increasing amount of the crop processed at home.

However, it must also be wary because the United States is the dominant buyer of canola oil, taking more than half of Canada’s production.

So Canadian crushers face risks from American policy on trade and renewable biofuel. This is not new, but in the age of president Donald Trump, it must cause some unease in corporate board rooms

The crushing industry is aware of the risks.

Federated Co-operatives and AGT Food and Ingredients in January 2025 shelved their plans for a $2 billion integrated canola crusher and renewable diesel plant in Regina, citing uncertain public policy and rising costs.

They did not detail the policy concerns, but uncertainty about access to the U.S. and its renewable fuel market must have been considerations.

However, other crushing plant builds and expansions went ahead.

Expansion continues despite risk

Louis Dreyfus and Cargill each added million tonne crushing capacities in the past year.

Those additions, plus strong utilization rates at existing plants, pushed canola processing in 2025-26 to 12.89 million tonnes, up almost 1.5 million, or 13 per cent, over the previous year.

The data is from Statistics Canada.

Canola oil production reached 5.48 million tonnes, up 13.7 percent.

Meal production reached 7.512 million tonnes, up 12 percent.

As this column was written, oil and meal export data for July was not available.

For the 11 months from August 2025 to June 2026, total canola oil exports stood at 3.1 million tonnes, up 1.8 percent over the same time last year.

Of that, 2.67 million tonnes, or 86 per cent went to the U.S.

That was up 10 percent from last year, when about 80 percent of all exports went to the U.S.

A large part of that goes to the renewable diesel market.

There has been much coverage here over the past year about the negotiations, lobbying and decisions in the U.S. regarding renewable fuel policy and how imported Canadian canola oil would fit into those new rules.

American agriculture celebrated the huge increases to biodiesel and renewable diesel blending mandates approved by the Environmental Protection Agency for 2026 and 2027.

That means much more vegetable oil, including canola, will go into fuel.

It marked a win for agriculture over those in the petroleum refining industry who lobby against increased biofuel mandates.

However, I wonder if any victory can be considered safe and unchangeable.

Diesel prices have soared since the U.S. and Israel started a war with Iran, restricting Middle East oil exports.

As crude prices rose, so did diesel and gasoline.

However, diesel soared even higher as Ukraine used drones and missiles to strike deep into Russia, degrading its refining infrastructure and causing it to stop exporting diesel.

Also, China reduced diesel exports, saving supply for its own needs.

There is not enough refining capacity in the rest of the world to replace these shortages.

While expensive gasoline angers the average motorist, the rise in diesel is a greater blow to the economy because it powers the trucks, trains and heavy equipment that keep farms and industry running.

That adds to inflation and the cost of living — key issues in this fall’s U.S.mid-term elections.

U.S. market is close, lucrative and vulnerable

The pressure on Trump to lower the cost of fuel is rising.

In this heated atmosphere, an opinion piece in the Washington Post Aug. 28 stands out.

Written by Derrick Morgan, executive vice-president of the Heritage Foundation, the piece, with the headline Good news, President Trump. You can slash gas prices yourself, argues that biofuel blending mandates push up fuel prices.

The Heritage Foundation is the right wing group behind Project 2025, the playbook that appears to have influenced much policy advanced by the Trump administration.

The foundation has long argued that policies promoting biofuel increase refining costs and discourage construction of new refineries.

Morgan says Trump could instruct the EPA to slash the blending mandates, which, he argues, would quickly drop the price at the pumps.

The piece was amplified by Republican senator Mike Lee of Utah, who promoted it on social media and launched his own attack on biofuel.

Biofuel supporters, including powerful senators from corn belt states, have prevailed over the Heritage Foundation’s critiques before, but with high fuel costs and inflation such a priority for voters, you never know what Trump might do to try to gain popularity.

Canadian crushers can’t abandon the U.S. market. It’s close and lucrative, but it is vulnerable.

The only way to reduce that vulnerability is to increase demand elsewhere.

Domestically, the industry must keep pressuring Ottawa to quickly implement its Sustainable Aviation Fuel plan and to ensure that Canada’s Clean Fuel program is driven by domestic supply.

text:
Australian industrial businesses considering thermal energy storage for process heat can use a new five-step framework designed to support early-stage technical and commercial assessments, according to HILT CRC.

Commissioned by the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA) and developed by the Heavy Industry Low-carbon Transition Cooperative Research Centre (HILT CRC), Thermal Energy Storage for Industrial Process Heat: A Practical Guide was officially launched by ARENA at the 2026 Australasian Renewable Heat Conference in Melbourne.

According to HILT CRC, Australian industry used 234 TWh of process heat in 2022–23, with more than 80 per cent supplied by fossil fuels and around 3 per cent electrified.

The guide is intended to help industrial managers assess whether thermal energy storage (TES) is suitable for their operations, compare it with other low-carbon heat technologies, evaluate system designs and integration options, consider electrical infrastructure requirements, and assess the commercial case for investment.

HILT CRC CEO Jenny Selway said the framework was designed to help businesses navigate what can be a complex investment decision.

“Companies looking to decarbonise process heat face a rapidly evolving range of technologies and vendors and it can be difficult to know where to start,” Selway said.

“The five-step framework provides a practical starting point. It helps businesses work systematically from understanding their own heat requirements through to process integration, infrastructure requirements, costs and ultimately the investment case.”

TES can store energy, including renewable electricity or waste heat, for use when industrial processes require heat. HILT CRC said assessing the technology requires consideration of a site’s thermal requirements, emissions objectives and overall costs.

Carl Christiansen, ARENA’s General Manager of Grid and Storage, said industrial heat represented a significant opportunity for emissions reduction.

“A large share of the heat used by Australian industry still comes from fossil fuels, so businesses need practical tools to assess lower-emissions alternatives,” Christiansen said.

Professor Joe Coventry of The Australian National University, who led development of the report’s technical content, said the assessment should begin with the requirements of the industrial process rather than a particular technology.

“The starting question shouldn’t be ‘Which thermal energy storage technology should we buy?’ It should be ‘What does our industrial process actually need?’” Coventry said.

The report includes Australian and international case studies, information on more than 30 medium- and high-temperature TES vendors, as well as identified risks, knowledge gaps and recommendations for industry, policymakers, regulators and investors.

Supporting appendices cover TES technologies and cost drivers, along with integration case studies involving electrical infrastructure, alumina refining and high-temperature waste heat in steelmaking. The report and related resources are available through the ARENA Knowledge Bank.
