text:
New Concepts Holdings (02221.HK) announced after market hours on September 3 that it plans to acquire a 70% stake in Anhui Feidian Environmental Technology for RMB 12.775 million (approximately HK$14.8949 million), to be fully settled through the issuance of consideration shares at HK$1 per share, representing a premium of approximately 78.51% over the closing price of HK$0.56 on the same day.

According to the announcement, New Concepts Holdings entered into equity transfer agreements with sellers Zhang Xiaoyun, Fang Shuo, and Zhu Zucun, acquiring 30%, 20%, and 20% stakes in Anhui Feidian Environmental Technology from the three parties respectively. The consideration will be settled through the allotment and issuance of approximately 14.8949 million consideration shares to the sellers in three tranches, with each consideration share priced at HK$1, representing a 78.51% premium over the closing price of HK$0.56 per share quoted on the Stock Exchange on the date of the equity transfer agreements (September 3).

The consideration shares represent approximately 6.50% of the company's issued share capital as of the announcement date, and approximately 6.10% of the enlarged issued share capital following the issuance of the consideration shares. The relevant shares will be allotted and issued under the general mandate without requiring shareholder approval, and once allotted and issued, will rank pari passu with existing issued shares.

Target Company Business Overview

Anhui Feidian Environmental Technology is primarily engaged in the collection, processing, and trading of waste oil. As of the announcement date, the company holds a 51% stake in Chuzhou Feidian Environmental Technology, which was newly established in July 2026 and will primarily engage in waste oil collection, processing, and trading business in China.

The board of New Concepts Holdings believes that the acquisition aligns with the group's development strategy of diversifying revenue sources and expanding its environmental protection business. Given the target company's established waste oil collection, processing, and trading capabilities in Anhui Province, along with its existing procurement network and customer base, the group can further expand its access to upstream waste oil resources upon completion of the acquisition.

Positioning in the Sustainable Aviation Fuel Supply Chain

The board noted that waste oil is a key raw material for producing sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and biodiesel. As the SAF industry continues to develop in China and globally, demand for compliant and traceable waste oil is expected to continue increasing. The acquisition enables the group to capitalize on opportunities arising from growing demand for renewable energy and low-carbon energy, further participate in this growth sector, and establish a stronger market position in the upstream segment of the renewable fuel supply chain.

The group currently operates multiple food waste treatment projects in Anhui Province, including in Hefei, Xuancheng, and Guoyang. These projects generate waste oil during operations, but the output from existing projects is limited. The board believes the acquisition will optimize the group's existing business by providing a mature waste oil collection, processing, and trading platform, which is expected to increase overall waste oil sales volume and broaden the revenue base.

Furthermore, given the geographic proximity of the target company's operations to the group's existing projects in Anhui Province, the acquisition is expected to facilitate operational coordination, improve logistics efficiency, optimize resource allocation, and strengthen procurement and sales capabilities. The board believes these synergies will help enhance the overall operational efficiency and competitiveness of the group's environmental protection business.

The acquisition is also part of the group's broader strategy to develop an integrated waste oil trading and distribution platform. By gradually consolidating waste oil from the group's existing projects and the acquired business, the group will be better positioned to drive quality control, procurement management, sales activities, and customer development efforts.

Transaction Structure and Market Observations

Issuing consideration shares at a premium of nearly 80% is a relatively uncommon arrangement in the Hong Kong stock market. Typically, buyers prefer to issue shares at a discount or at par to settle acquisition consideration, reflecting a liquidity discount on the shares. New Concepts Holdings' decision to issue consideration shares at HK$1 per share, a 78.51% premium to the market price, indicates that the sellers have higher pricing requirements for the consideration shares, or reflects positive expectations from both parties regarding the group's future development prospects.

From a share dilution perspective, the consideration shares represent approximately 6.10% of the enlarged share capital, resulting in a relatively moderate dilution impact on existing shareholders. Since the consideration shares can be issued without shareholder approval, the execution risk of completing the transaction primarily depends on whether the conditions precedent set out in the equity transfer agreements can be satisfied.

New Concepts Holdings' acquisition rationale is clear: using shares as the payment instrument to extend its business reach into the upstream segment of waste oil collection and trading without depleting cash reserves. This creates vertical integration with the group's established food waste treatment projects in Anhui Province, helping to connect the complete chain from waste oil generation, collection, and processing to trading.

It is worth noting that Chuzhou Feidian Environmental Technology, held by the target company, was only established in July 2026 and has an extremely short operating history. Investors should pay attention to whether this newly established subsidiary can rapidly build a stable waste oil procurement network and customer base, and whether its integration with the group's existing business can generate the expected synergies on schedule.

title: Sri Lanka, Nepal trade team visits Kansas soybean farm - High Plains Journal
description:

Haselwood has attended Soy Connext for several years because of his involvement with international promotion of U.S. soy.
According to Kansas Soybean, in 2026 about 400 international buyers from 67 countries were in attendance at the soy event.
Most visitors are container importers meaning they allow preserved shipments of food-grade U.S. soy.
Sri Lanka is the top U.S. soybean meal market in South Asia, feeding their large poultry population.
text:
Bob Haselwood recently opened his farm to visitors from Sri Lanka and Nepal.

The team was visiting in conjunction with Soy Connext, the U.S. Soybean Export Council’s annual global event that connects buyers, sellers, growers and other industry partners.

Haselwood has been a member of the Kansas Soybean Commission for 21 years and has hosted many trade teams. He said the farm’s location between Manhattan and Kansas City makes it an ideal stop.

“I couldn’t tell you how many teams we’ve hosted over the years,” he said. “Whether they’ve come through USSEC or IGP, we’ve had plenty of that here.”

Haselwood believes this is the first group that he’s had from Sri. Lanka and Nepal.

“We’ve had people from Japan and China and parts of Europe and out of the Americas,” he said. “We’ve hit about every region, but that area (of) South Asia, and I don’t think we’ve had anybody from there.”

Overall, the response was positive.

“It’s always good to talk about the things that we do, and I mean we hope that we’re doing things sustainably,” Haselwood said. “We did talk about that, and then they asked about production costs and what type of yields we get and things like that.”

For him, visits like this are important.

“I think a lot of the people want to see what we’re doing in the U.S., so they kind of get an idea what’s going on with our products,” Haselwood said. “We’re in soy products, and why we’ve had better quality than, say, another supplier.”

It works the same when another Kansas farmer or United States farmer visits another country.

“The buyers always like to show what they’re doing too, so it’s a I guess it works in reverse too,” he said.

Haselwood has attended Soy Connext for several years because of his involvement with international promotion of U.S. soy. According to Kansas Soybean, in 2026 about 400 international buyers from 67 countries were in attendance at the soy event. This is a strong indicator of U.S. soy’s value in global markets.

USSEC plans the trade teams before and after Soy Connext in an effort to get every international visitor on a farm and in front of a farmer before they leave. Most visitors are container importers meaning they allow preserved shipments of food-grade U.S. soy. Containers give these countries the flexibility to ship to small ports or landlocked countries like Nepal, Haselwood said.

Officials at Kansas Soybean said attendees were employed in roles like CEO, managing director, or financial controller, and the vast majority were from poultry feeding operations, though others included feed manufacturers and one crush plant. A couple of journalists—one each form Nepal and Sri Lanka—were taking the stories of U.S. farming back with them.

Sri Lanka is the top U.S. soybean meal market in South Asia, feeding their large poultry population. Soy from the U.S. holds about an 87% market share of soybean meal imports to Sri Lanka, even with disadvantages to other countries like India because of taxes and import duties. Nepal is landlocked and often imports raw ingredients for feed. Demand for meat and eggs is expected to double in the next decade with 91% of their whole soybean imports coming from the U.S.

Haselwood is encouraged by the U.S. Department of Agriculture crop production numbers that came out recently, showing an increase in acres for soybeans. He said when looking at the U.S. crop, traditionally about half of it was exported, sometimes nearly 60% was shipped out. Crush expansion has pushed that number further.

“The last I heard, the U.S. has a capacity to crush 60% of the crop, so that would only leave 40% for export,” he said. “You listen to different economists and whatever, and some suggest there could be things that some of the crushers can do to add capacity to the plants, without major things, and we could move it up—the amount that we were able to crush.”

The added crush capacity will leave more soybean meal and oil to “do something with,” he said.

“Of course, right now with the new renewable volume obligations for renewable fuels, that’s put a go signal for everyone to produce more biodiesel and renewable diesel,” he said. “So that is going to take up some of that. “There’ll be more meal to export or be consumed domestically.”

“Some of these countries that we don’t think about exporting soybeans or meal or oil to, some of those countries—the younger generation comes on, they’re trying to eat more protein, and animal protein is what they’re looking at, and that’s why they’re going to need more meal,” Haselwood said.

The farm

Haselwood’s nephew, Ryan Johnson, has taken over the majority of the acres on the farm and after farming with him for the last eight years. This helps Haselwood to continue to do the work on the checkoff boards, but the soybean crop in 2026 is looking good.

“Well, we were very fortunate. We had ample rain through June and July, and I think Ryan told me the other day that we had 6 inches, or a little over 6 inches of rain in July, and almost two of those came in the last two days of July,” he said. “We’re only a couple of weeks from a big rain, and then actually last week I think we got four-tenths.”

But some of the beans during the tour had smaller pods, he said, and that’s not something Haselwood likes to see.

“There’s a lot of little bitty pods. They’re just past bloom and if it stays hot like this, some of them are going to just drop. They’ll abort those and just fall off,” he said. “Last year we had. I think Ryan said we averaged 65 or 66 bushels per acre off everything he had, and we’re not expecting that kind of yield.”

Johnson is aiming for 50 bushels per acre, but Haselwood said, “ask me again in two weeks.”

Harvest isn’t moved up like wheat or corn crops, but instead the soybeans work off the length of night and reach maturity on their own time.

“If it stays hot, they might decide to quit. Fill what they can, drop some of the pods, and then go ahead and mature,” he said.

Board member

Haselwood got his start in the organization as a Kansas Soybean Commission member, after being asked to apply to fill an open seat in the eighth district. A few years later he got appointed to the United Soybean Board and served 10 years, with one being a chair of the USB. He’s also serving on the Clean Fuels America Alliance.

“Which is basically the same board that promotes biodiesel, renewable diesel, and sustainable aviation fuel,” he said. “I’ve been serving on their governing board—it’ll be two years in November.”

For him, serving on the boards is rewarding.

“When you see that soybean growth in just not only acres but yield in soybeans and the fact that we’re using so many more soybeans, whether it’s through feed or alternative uses or fuel, it makes you think that we’re doing something right,” he said.

He looks at it like—if they weren’t doing something right, people wouldn’t want to plant more soybeans.

“And because they can make a profit, if everything’s right, they’re more profitable than some of the other crops, and so I feel like that’s why when serving on these checkoff boards, that we’ve invested the money wisely, because I don’t think people would be so enthused about planting it.”

text:
Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) is expected to deliver around 65% of the emissions reductions needed by 2050 to achieve the airline industry's net-zero goal.

Despite its critical role, SAF supply remains constrained, concentrated in a few locations, and costs 2 to 5 times more than conventional aviation fuel (CAF).

A pragmatic solution is to decouple the physical fuel from its environmental attributes (EAs), allowing airlines and their customers to claim SAF-use regardless of where the fuel is produced, delivered, or consumed. For example, an airline in Asia can pay for and claim the EAs of a particular batch of SAF that might be produced and uplifted in the United States. This approach is known as book-and-claim.

The integrity of book-and-claim requires the EAs linked to a specific SAF batch to be tracked transparently after they are split from the physical fuel so that they are counted and claimed only once. SAF registries, such as the CADO SAF Registry, provide this tracking and accounting mechanism.

In a typical book-and-claim transaction, the registry becomes involved after the SAF has been blended with CAF and delivered to a point of no return, such as an airport fuel farm, available for uplift by any airline. The supplier surrenders the sustainability documentation to the registry and transfers the associated EAs through the registry to the purchasing airline, which redeems them, i.e., burns them virtually. The registry issues a certificate proving the airline’s ownership of the EAs and right to claim against them. Any airline customers involved in the transaction also receive a certificate to substantiate their emissions reporting.

In this way, book-and-claim helps the global SAF market to leapfrog local physical supply constraints and immature supply chains. This gives producers access to more airlines and more airlines gain access to SAF, increasing competition, and lowering costs. This is key to accelerating the decarbonization of air transport and building this new energy market faster. Regulators can provide this instrumental support by the stroke of the pen, including under the EU ETS, and help expand the SAF market and attract investors.

text:
Singapore will introduce a new Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) levy for departing air passengers from January 1, 2027, adding another charge to airline tickets as the city-state accelerates its aviation decarbonization efforts.

The levy will apply to tickets and air services sold from October 1, 2026. Airlines will be required to show it as a separate line item in the fare breakdown, alongside existing taxes and charges.

The charge will depend on the destination and cabin class. Economy and premium economy passengers will pay between S$1 and S$10.40 (about US$0.78-$8.15) each way, while business and first-class travelers will pay four times those amounts.

For a direct flight from Singapore, the economy-class levy will be S$1 (US$0.78) to Southeast Asia, S$2.80 (US$2.19) to Northeast and South Asia or Australia, S$6.40 (US$5.01) to Europe, and S$10.40 (US$8.15) to the Americas.

Premium-cabin charges range from S$4 (US$3.13) to S$41.60 (US$32.55).

The levy applies to passengers beginning their journey in Singapore. Travelers simply connecting through the city are excluded.

Singapore has set a 1% SAF uplift target for 2027, with plans to increase the share to between 3% and 5% by 2030, depending on global market conditions and SAF availability. Sustainable aviation fuel can reduce lifecycle carbon emissions by up to 80% compared with conventional jet fuel.

The funds will be placed into a statutory SAF Fund and used to purchase SAF and related environmental attributes, as well as cover administrative costs.

The Singapore Sustainable Aviation Fuel Company Ltd. (SAFCo), a nonprofit company wholly owned by the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (CAAS), will collect the levy. It will also oversee SAF procurement, accounting and allocation of the associated environmental attributes.

title: The next disruptor is already here: AFPM Summit panel grades five years of energy transition bets
description:

Renewable diesel and renewable natural gas delivered close to what was promised, riding existing pipeline, terminal and storage infrastructure to market fast enough to capture incentive windows before they closed.
Audience questions steered the conversation toward the newest disruptor in the room: AI and data center power demand.
And asked to sum up the industry's response to the last five years in one word, Orr landed on "chaotic," McCaffrey on something closer to over-exuberant.
text:
By: Catherine Watkins, Hydrocarbon Processing

The 2026 AFPM Summit brought roughly 1,500 refining and petrochemical professionals to Grapevine, Texas (U.S.) this year, the largest turnout the event has seen in several years. Early on Day Two, a packed sustainability-track session took the unusual step of grading the industry's own homework: "The Next Energy Market Disruptor Is Coming. Are We Ready? Lessons from the Last Five Years' Key Projects," moderated by Brian Boeger of Axens North America, with Daniel Orr of Worley Consulting and Meaghan McCaffrey of Burns & McDonnell's 1898 & Co. as speakers.

Orr opened by tracing how capital moved. Pre-pandemic, projects were underwritten the old-fashioned way, on throughput and margin improvement using conventional market pricing. Somewhere around 2016, renewable diesel programs and tightening state and federal incentives started pulling investments toward clean energy, and COVID accelerated that shift into a full trend line: by 2025, clean energy had grown to roughly 65% of energy-sector investment against fossil fuel's 35%, a rough mirror image of 2015.

McCaffrey then walked the room through a technology-by-technology scorecard comparing 2021's expectations to 2026's reality. Renewable diesel and renewable natural gas delivered close to what was promised, riding existing pipeline, terminal and storage infrastructure to market fast enough to capture incentive windows before they closed. Carbon capture made real progress but slower than advertised, dragged down by permitting and pipeline buildout. Hydrogen and blue and green ammonia were the biggest letdowns: most U.S. hydrogen projects were delayed or canceled outright, and of roughly 80 ammonia projects McCaffrey had tracked, only a handful were actually built. Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) landed somewhere in between, hampered less by demand than by a policy gap.

From there, the panel pivoted to what discipline should look like next time: avoid final investment decision (FID) paralysis, pursue renewables selectively rather than everywhere at once, anchor projects in real regional demand, keep capital discipline, treat project fundamentals as hard gates rather than checkboxes and get ahead of supply chain risk instead of assuming compressors and transformers will show up on schedule. Orr's practical add was to pull logistics studies, red-flag reviews, and feedstock and offtake agreements much earlier into the process, ideally within six to eight weeks of project kickoff, rather than discovering fatal risks after a board has already been pitched.

Audience questions steered the conversation toward the newest disruptor in the room: AI and data center power demand. Both speakers said client conversations now start with power availability and offtake on day one, that OEM track record and supply chain queue position are now front-loaded discussions, and that skilled labor, not just equipment, is becoming a genuine bottleneck as construction crews get pulled between data center builds and traditional refining and petrochemical work.

A couple of things stood out. First, the panelists flagged that the same tax credit economics drew wildly mismatched players into the same lane, from multibillion-dollar multinationals down to literal one-person shops working out of a garage, all chasing identical incentives with very different capacity to execute. Second, despite a summer 2026 record for daily U.S. air travel, SAF volumes are still lagging targets mainly because the policy underpinning renewable diesel's success, a federal blending mandate known as the Renewable Volume Obligation, has no real equivalent for SAF; airlines want it, refiners can build it, but the demand-side mandate that made renewable diesel pencil just isn't there yet. And asked to sum up the industry's response to the last five years in one word, Orr landed on "chaotic," McCaffrey on something closer to over-exuberant. Their word for what comes next: cautiously optimistic.

title: What if batteries make flying cheaper? A 30-seat electric plane just flew for $5. Decarbonized aviation
description:
Decarbonized aviation was meant to be mainly a Hydrogen and Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) story.
But that still raises two really important questions in my mind: 1️⃣ Could "decarbonising aviation" actually drive down short-haul flight prices?
2️⃣ If electrification can help with short-haul flights, be it as full electric or hybrid, can we then concentrate Sustainable Aviation Fuel volumes onto the long-hauls in the future?
And if that happens will Hydrogen be squeezed out as an onboard aviation fuel altogether, given its cost and storage challenges?
❓ Do you think Batteries can play a significant role in short-haul aviation?
text: What if batteries make flying cheaper? A 30-seat electric plane just flew for $5. Decarbonized aviation was meant to be mainly a Hydrogen and Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) story. But now, surprisingly enough, batteries seem to be becoming a much more serious third player. And that is really significant: Almost half of all global flight departures are under 1,000 km - creating a potentially huge target for some degree of electrification... ...because batteries are relentlessly improving in energy density per kg or pound, while moving down the cost curve. So, now a new test flight has just climbed to 1,100 feet for just around $5 as shown in the below video by The Independent. Ok - the 30 passenger seats were empty, with only the test pilot aboard, but adding the passengers isn't going to suddenly turn roughly $5 of electricity into a much larger number. And ok - a real commercial flight would fly further and higher and carry a full payload with reserves, so $5 is obviously not the electricity cost of a commercial passenger flight. But that still raises two really important questions in my mind: 1️⃣ Could "decarbonising aviation" actually drive down short-haul flight prices? If electrification could help with short-haul distances might these become actually cheaper than they are now? Like are we talking green discount and not green premium here down the line? That would be revolutionary to say the least - and it might happen. 2️⃣ If electrification can help with short-haul flights, be it as full electric or hybrid, can we then concentrate Sustainable Aviation Fuel volumes onto the long-hauls in the future? And if that happens will Hydrogen be squeezed out as an onboard aviation fuel altogether, given its cost and storage challenges? It already did not look good for Hydrogen in aviation compared to years past, given the announced delays and cost challenges... ... so it might be that we are back to two players when it comes to leading technology options: Sustainable Aviation Fuels and Batteries. ❓ Do you think Batteries can play a significant role in short-haul aviation? ♻️ Repost this to broaden the conversation. 👉 Follow Nik Baumann for more.

text:
MotionMiners GmbH has been named the winner of the Lufthansa Cargo Innovation Award 2026. The technology company impressed the jury with its Motion-Mining technology, which uses wearables, sensors, and AI-powered data analysis to automatically capture and evaluate manual work processes. The Innovation Pitches were launched by startup accelerator HAUS61 in 2025 and were held again as part of this year’s Air Cargo Conference 2026.

Frank Bauer, Chief Operating Officer of Lufthansa Cargo, served as a member of the award jury. The award was presented by Heike Wörner, Head of Business Development at Lufthansa Cargo, to Christoph Dorra, Sales Team Lead at MotionMiners.

“People, technology, and complex operational processes are closely interconnected in air cargo. MotionMiners has convincingly demonstrated how modern sensor technology can provide transparency into real-world processes within a very short time while taking local conditions into account. In addition to its potential to improve efficiency and ergonomics, the solution’s high level of employee acceptance was particularly compelling to the jury. This combination of rapid implementation, reliable data, and close alignment with operational realities makes the solution especially relevant to air cargo,” said Wörner.

A total of around 30 logistics startups applied to participate in the Innovation Pitch. Eight were selected as finalists and presented their solutions live at the Air Cargo Conference before the jury and an audience of industry professionals. MotionMiners prevailed with a practical approach that combines data-driven process optimization with more ergonomic workflows.

“Air cargo is a highly relevant growth market for MotionMiners. Handling involves numerous complex and labor-intensive processes where our technology can identify concrete opportunities for improvement, from walking and driving routes to waiting times and ergonomic strain. The Lufthansa Cargo Innovation Award provides a strong starting point for us to establish ourselves in the industry,” said Dorra.

Sensor technology provides transparency into manual processes

For the analysis, employees and material handling equipment are temporarily fitted with sensors. Beacon transmitters also enable the captured activities to be assigned to specific locations. The data is analyzed anonymously on the web-based MotionMiners Process Intelligence platform. This makes it possible to identify time-consuming process steps, unnecessary travel, waiting times, and ergonomic strain. For material handling equipment, the analysis can also examine utilization, empty trips, and material flows. MotionMiners offers its technology both through consulting projects and under a licensing model that enables companies to conduct their own analyses.

By winning the Lufthansa Cargo Innovation Award, MotionMiners highlights the importance of data-driven process analysis in advancing complex air cargo and logistics operations.

About MotionMiners

MotionMiners GmbH, headquartered in Dortmund, Germany, develops technologies for the automated analysis of manual work processes. Founded in 2017, the company combines wearable sensors and other hardware components with its web-based MotionMiners Process Intelligence software. The solution anonymously captures and analyzes movement and process data from employees and vehicles, revealing opportunities to improve efficiency and ergonomics. Its technology is used in industries including logistics, manufacturing, automotive, and retail. The company is also exploring how robotic systems can benefit from knowledge of manual work processes.

Trump’s intervention amplifies pressure on Britain’s government over two politically salient vulnerabilities: high energy costs and irregular migration. It also exposes an increasingly strained UK-U.S. relationship, with Trump urging a more fossil-fuel-led policy direction.

Trump frames net zero as a driver of excessive energy prices and advocates further development of North Sea oil and gas. However, this is primarily political messaging rather than a detailed policy assessment: the government maintains that a transition to cleaner electricity remains necessary as it considers two major North Sea projects.

On migration, Trump’s rhetoric aligns with a domestic issue already strengthening Reform UK, despite government claims that small-boat crossings have recently fallen through action against launch networks and smuggling gangs.

AI tech rally lifts Wall Street despite oil and rate risks

Wall Street rebounded as AI-linked technology strength and stabilising Treasury yields outweighed immediate oil-market anxiety, but the rally looks fragile ahead of U.S. employment and inflation data. The S&P 500 gained 0.5%, the Dow 0.6% and Nasdaq 0.5%; Dell surged 15.8% on stronger AI-computing demand, while Nvidia rose 3.2%.

The market is effectively pricing a tug-of-war, where AI CAPEX (capital expenditure) remains a powerful earnings catalyst, but higher energy prices and yields threaten margins, consumer purchasing power, and inflation expectations. And with Brent settling at $95.63/bbl (price per barrel) as the Iran conflict and Strait of Hormuz disruption continue, the 10-year Treasury yield stayed elevated at 4.78%.

For investors, Friday’s jobs report and next week’s inflation data are the near-term catalysts. A weak labour reading alongside persistent inflation would complicate the Fed’s choices and could revive bond volatility, putting high-valuation technologies back under pressure despite AI’s strong fundamentals.

Asia bolsters oil and gas buffers after Hormuz shock

The Strait of Hormuz disruption is accelerating an Asian energy-security pivot, as countries are expanding strategic oil and LNG storage, domestic pipelines and supplier-linked overseas reserves to reduce vulnerability to a single maritime chokepoint.

Japan’s proposed $10 billion POWERR Asia initiative, India’s planned 13-million-barrel addition, potential South Korean reserve expansion, and China’s pipeline/LNG build-out illustrate a regional shift from “just-in-time imports” to resilience infrastructure. The immediate winner is storage and midstream investment; Gulf producers also benefit by placing barrels nearer Asian demand centres. However, more stockpiles mitigate short disruptions rather than address structural import dependence: several Southeast Asian states remain below the IEA’s 90-day benchmark, while new fossil infrastructure can create cost and transition-risk lock-in. The strategic test is whether governments pair buffers with demand reduction, efficiency, renewables and diversified supply routes, not simply larger oil tanks.

text:
Singapore defers cargo green jet fuel levy until 2028

Singapore will introduce a green jet-fuel levy for departing passengers from January 1, 2027, and will postpone the air-cargo levy until January 1, 2028. This preserves the country’s sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) strategy but acknowledges that cargo charging is more complex and commercially sensitive than passenger ticketing.

From October 1, 2026, passengers will pay S$1–S$10.40 in economy/premium economy and S$4–S$41.60 in business/first class, depending on distance and cabin. Revenue will fund SAF purchases, socializing part of aviation’s decarbonization costs rather than leaving airlines to bear the full fuel premium. Passenger levies fit within existing booking systems and are modest enough not to deter demand at Singapore’s Changi Airport. Higher charges for longer routes reflect greater fuel consumption, while premium-cabin fees align with the greater space and emissions per passenger.

Cargo is harder, as costs flow through airlines, forwarders and shippers under bespoke contracts, creating uncertainty over collection and incidence. The deferral gives the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (CAAS) time to build an operationally credible mechanism rather than a symbolic one.

Delaying cargo charges protects Changi’s short-term freight competitiveness but leaves a major, business-funded SAF demand channel unpriced for another year, potentially slowing early procurement certainty. The levy embeds SAF costs in fares, but the small fee won’t materially change flying behavior; its value is fiscal rather than in direct emissions reductions.

Singapore is testing whether it can become a regional SAF-demand hub without diverting traffic. If the model works, it could set a template for other global aviation hubs. However, if charges rise before SAF supply scales, competitiveness and carbon-leakage risks will intensify.

Brussels has cleared two separate State aid decisions: a €30 million Portuguese scheme to cushion agriculture, fisheries and aquaculture firms against elevated fuel and fertilizer costs, and a German capacity mechanism from 2031 worth up to €35 billion to guarantee electricity supply.

For Portugal, the measure offers near-term relief to food-system producers but risks entrenching fossil-fuel exposure unless tied to efficiency or fuel-switching, while likely easing short-term price pass-through to consumers.

In Germany, the approval signals sustained reliance on capacity payments to preserve generator margins, shaping investor expectations around gas peakers versus storage and demand-side response and potentially crowding out some pure energy-only market revenues.

At the EU level, this wave of ad hoc, sector-specific aid could complicate the Green Deal and REPowerEU narrative unless explicitly framed as transitional and conditioned on decarbonization.

text:
Gasoline blended with 15% ethanol, known as E15, helps build demand for U.S.-grown crops, particularly corn. However, the impact that E15 can have on domestic demand for corn depends on policy decisions, fuel use trends and overall grain market conditions.

E15 is not new, but its year-round availability currently varies by market and relies on annual summer approvals. These federal fuel rules, as well as retail infrastructure and consumer demand, all influence whether E15 can be accessed at the pump. Those factors matter because ethanol is a major domestic market for corn and an important part of the rural economy.

Ethanol is a key market for U.S. corn

Ethanol production is one of the largest domestic uses of corn. According to the U.S. Department of Agriculture Economic Research Service, U.S. corn used for fuel ethanol totaled 5.4 billion bushels, representing about a third of national corn production. The USDA also reported that U.S. fuel ethanol exports reached a record 2.19 billion gallons during the same marketing year.

Demand for ethanol has remained relatively stable even as U.S. production has increased. At the same time, total corn supply has grown, including recent crop years exceeding 18.6 billion bushels, contributing to higher corn inventory and pressure on crop prices.

Ethanol represents one of the largest and most consistent domestic demand drivers for American farmers.

At the same time, U.S. gasoline demand is forecasted to gradually decline over the long term due to improved fuel efficiency and vehicle electrification. Higher blends like E15 can influence how much ethanol — and therefore corn — is used within a smaller total fuel market.

Ethanol also produces feed and fuel byproducts

The ethanol value chain extends beyond fuel. Ethanol production also generates byproducts used in livestock feed and other markets.

The Renewable Fuels Association, a major trade association representing ethanol producers, estimated that U.S. ethanol biorefineries produced more than 35 million metric tons of feed byproducts in 2025, including distillers grains, corn gluten feed and corn gluten meal. These products are used by beef, dairy, swine and poultry producers.

Ethanol production also generates distillers corn oil, which is used in renewable diesel, biodiesel, sustainable aviation fuel and animal feed markets.

What to watch

E15 availability will continue to be shaped by several factors:

Federal and state fuel policy: EPA waivers and state-level fuel rules currently determine where and when E15 can be sold, but if Congress would pass a nationwide year-round E15 law, it would provide more certainty for retailers.

Retail infrastructure investments: Adding E15 as an option at a retail station may require capital investment in compatible storage tanks and dispensers, compliance with labeling requirements and available supply at nearby bulk fuel terminals.

Consumer awareness and education: Drivers need clear information about vehicle compatibility, fuel pricing and product labeling.

Corn supply and ethanol economics: Corn prices, ethanol margins, gasoline demand and export markets all influence ethanol production and demand.

Broader renewable fuels policy: Policies affecting renewable diesel, biodiesel, sustainable aviation fuel and low-carbon fuel markets can also affect demand for agricultural feedstocks, including corn oil and soybean oil.

Bottom line: E15 is good for U.S. farmers

Growth in E15 is important to U.S. farmers because it can expand domestic demand for U.S.-grown corn. The size of that impact depends on consistent policy, retail availability, fuel economics and consumer adoption.

As E15 policy grows in priority for legislators, more retailers offer E15 and more consumers understand when and how to use it, higher ethanol blends can play a larger role in connecting U.S. crop production with domestic energy demand.

title: Electrified cars put Brazil's gasoline, ethanol demand under pressure - Valor International
description:
“In every study we’ve done, we end up at this point [of declining fuel demand].
Because the greater the penetration of electric vehicles, the more consumption will fall,” said Marcel Martin, director-general of ICCT Brazil.
Although still modest in aggregate terms, the erosion of ethanol and gasoline demand is likely to accelerate in Brazil, Citi said.
As a result, electrified vehicles accounted for 21.1% of total vehicle sales in July.
According to Citi’s calculations, electrified vehicles would account for 11% of Brazil’s vehicle fleet by 2030 under a scenario in which they represent 37% of new-vehicle sales.
text:
Rapid growth in electric vehicle sales in Brazil is beginning to affect demand for gasoline and ethanol, a trend expected to intensify over the next two decades, according to expert estimates. A Citi study estimates that 700 million liters of fuel—specifically ethanol and gasoline—were not consumed in Brazil last year because of the use of electrified vehicles, including electric and hybrid models. The amount was equivalent to 1% of domestic demand in 2025.

Citi says the shift is structural and long-term. Based on a projected 1.8% increase in gross domestic product (GDP) over the 2025-2026 period, the bank expects consumption of fuels used by vehicles with internal-combustion engines—a category that includes ethanol and gasoline and is known as the Otto cycle—to grow at a rate equivalent to roughly 120% of GDP growth. Starting in 2027, however, the trend is expected to reverse, with demand declining even as GDP expands.

Stellantis reshapes Brazil strategy as Chinese EV rivals gain ground

Brazil becomes world’s top importer of Chinese cars

Analysis: Chinese automakers defy Henry Ford’s principle

Plug-in models drive Brazil’s electric vehicle boom

Electrified vehicles gain ground at Brazil’s rental companies

Similarly, scenarios developed by the nongovernmental organization ICCT Brazil point to a gradual decline in fuel consumption through 2050, even under a scenario of moderate electrification of the vehicle fleet. “In every study we’ve done, we end up at this point [of declining fuel demand]. Because the greater the penetration of electric vehicles, the more consumption will fall,” said Marcel Martin, director-general of ICCT Brazil.

Although still modest in aggregate terms, the erosion of ethanol and gasoline demand is likely to accelerate in Brazil, Citi said. In the bank’s most likely scenario, the volume of ethanol and gasoline “displaced”—that is, fuel that is no longer consumed because of the use of electric and hybrid vehicles—will reach 5 billion liters in 2030, equivalent to 8% of actual demand. By 2040, that share is expected to rise to 14%, or 9 billion liters.

“There is already an impact on fuel consumption from these electrified vehicles,” said Gabriel Barra, a Citi analyst who authored the study with Pedro Gama and Pedro Ferreira de Mello. “When we look at the longer-term scenarios, one important point is the penetration we’re seeing in Brazil today: it is high [in terms of] sales of electrified cars,” he added.

In July, registrations of electric and hybrid vehicles totaled just over 56,000 units, nearly three times the number sold in the same month of 2025, according to data from the Brazilian Electric Vehicle Association (ABVE). As a result, electrified vehicles accounted for 21.1% of total vehicle sales in July.

Despite their growing share of new-vehicle sales, electrified vehicles represented only 1.3% of Brazil’s light-vehicle fleet at the end of 2025, according to U.S. consulting firm Integrate Data Facts (IDF).

The sales boom is directly related to the decline in electric vehicle prices in Brazil. In 2012, when the first imported electrified car launched in the country, it cost about 8.5 times as much as an internal-combustion vehicle. Today, the difference is about 1.3 times, according to Citi.

“Here [in Brazil], what matters is price. So, if a car in the same category is a little cheaper, it sells. That’s what the Chinese are all about,” said Edmar de Almeida, a professor and researcher at the Energy Institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro (PUC-Rio).

Of the 15 best-selling electrified car models in Brazil in July, 14 were made by Chinese automakers, according to data compiled by ABVE. Together, the 14 models accounted for nearly 62.5% of sales in the category during the month.

Although the import tariff on electrified vehicles assembled outside Brazil rose to 35% in July, Citi does not see tariffs as an obstacle likely to significantly slow the arrival of Chinese cars in the country. This is because quotas were established for completely knocked-down (CKD) and semi-knocked-down (SKD) vehicles. In addition, Chinese automakers are beginning to produce vehicles in Brazil.

Another factor weighing on fuel demand is the adoption of electric and hybrid light vehicles by commercial fleets, including taxis and cars used by ride-hailing services. Under Citi’s model, these drivers travel an average of 48,000 kilometers a year, six times more than conventional drivers, who travel 8,000 kilometers a year.

“When you have this small level of penetration, but among consumers who drive these cars a lot, the impact is significant. You have a multiplier effect: even though the percentage of the fleet is small, it is amplified by consumption that is much higher than that of the rest of the fleet,” Barra said.

A third factor highlighted by Citi analysts is the stagnation in the fuel efficiency of the internal-combustion fleet. The most efficient model among the 10 best-selling vehicles in the country achieved about 16 kilometers per liter around 2016. Today, the figure is approximately 15 kilometers per liter.

Taking the weighted average of the 10 market-leading models, fuel efficiency of internal-combustion vehicles improved by about 16% over the seven years through 2016, but by only about 2% over the following nine years.

An ICCT study on decarbonizing road transportation projects a significant reduction in energy consumption—particularly gasoline, ethanol, and diesel—under “moderate” (-14.5%) and “ambitious” (-41.5%) electrification scenarios between 2025 and 2050, despite a 27% increase in the size of the vehicle fleet.

In the NGO’s view, a moderate scenario would be one in which sales of battery-electric vehicles were in line with those in other Latin American countries, reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 28% between 2025 and 2050. The ambitious scenario, meanwhile, is based on the assumption of an accelerated transition to zero-emission vehicles, with a focus on battery-electric models.

The transition, however, is far from posing a threat to the fuel industry in either the short or medium term. “Fuel use, whether ethanol or fossil fuel, will continue for a long time. There is a transition, and it won’t happen overnight,” Martin of ICCT Brazil said. According to Citi’s calculations, electrified vehicles would account for 11% of Brazil’s vehicle fleet by 2030 under a scenario in which they represent 37% of new-vehicle sales.

As for ethanol, Edmar de Almeida of PUC-Rio sees the possibility of redirecting the product to markets outside the automotive sector. “I don’t believe this will be a long-term problem because ethanol has other markets, especially SAF [sustainable aviation fuel],” the academic said. “If you have excess ethanol, you can convert it into aviation fuel.”

The National Union of Fuel and Lubricant Distributors (Sindicom) and Ipiranga declined to comment when contacted about the effects of electrification of Brazil’s light-vehicle fleet on gasoline and ethanol consumption.

Vibra said by email that it “is monitoring the evolution of mobility in Brazil and understands that electrification will play an increasingly important role in the coming years.” The company stressed, however, that Brazil’s dynamics differ from those seen in other markets and are likely to be characterized by the coexistence of different technologies and energy solutions.

text:
CP AXTRA Public Company Limited (SET: CPAXT or CP AXTRA), the operator of Makro and Lotus’s, is advancing its “Happy & Healthy Mall” strategy with plans to develop and renovate 60 projects across 29 provinces nationwide in 2026–2027. The strategy will transform hypermarkets from traditional retail spaces into key traffic anchors for shopping malls, helping attract visitors while connecting shopping, dining, lifestyle, and experiences under one roof. Closer integration between hypermarkets and mall space is designed to support and drive mutual growth, while meeting the evolving lifestyle needs of modern consumers.

The hypermarket will help connect various elements across the four pillars of the strategy: Food Destination, Lifestyle, Wellness, and Sustainability. Year-round partner campaigns, exclusive privileges, and Events & Entertainment are intended to increase both visit frequency and dwell time, giving mall tenants greater exposure and access to a wider customer base.

CP AXTRA is further elevating its hypermarkets as Fresh Food Destinations, by expanding product variety by more than 50,000 items, with a greater focus on fresh food, ready-to-eat products, and bakery offerings. The bakery offering also features Artisan Bakery, a carefully crafted range of baked goods made through traditional methods and using quality ingredients, including French butter, to deliver a naturally rich taste and aroma. An Open Kitchen layout gives customers direct sight of food preparation, and dishes featured in Hidden Taste Thailand Presented by Lotus’s are being added to in-store menus. A wider selection of Own Brand products and imported goods will further position hypermarkets as more than places to shop, but as starting points for food and lifestyle experiences.

The company is also modernizing the in-store experience through data-driven and AI-powered Retail Tech. text:
When Scott Kirby arrived at United, he says there was talk of the airline pulling out of Denver. A decade later, United is growing its presence here – in terms of flights and pilot training. It is already the largest carrier at Denver International Airport, with Southwest and Frontier a distant second and third.

“The Denver hub does really, really well for us,” Kirby said, fresh off an appearance Wednesday at the Denver Metro Chamber of Commerce’s annual meeting. “It’s amazing. When I first got to United, somebody suggested closing the Denver hub. Wall Street was pressuring us to do that. Fortunately, we didn’t.”

Clad in a blue suit reminiscent of the airline’s livery, the 58-year-old Air Force Academy graduate offered his takes on airfares, wages, artificial intelligence and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

The following interview with Colorado Matters Senior Host Ryan Warner has been lightly edited.

Ryan Warner: United already added simulators to its flight training center in Central Park, and I gather you're kind of landlocked there. Will you help us picture what you're building at Denver International Airport?

Scott Kirby: So on the land that we bought near the airport, the first thing we're doing is building more simulators. We have over a hundred acres, so we'll build more in the years to come, but having more simulators, even though the training center we have today is the biggest in the world, we're growing faster, we're bigger than any airline in the world, and we're growing faster than any airline in history has ever done, which means we need even more.

Warner: So that's both a function of adding pilots, and then obviously as that grows, that training needs to be maintained.

Kirby: Yeah. So when we hire a new pilot, they have two months of training. Anytime someone transitions from one fleet to another — you fly a 737 and switch to a plane in the A320 family or you switch to 787, whatever it is — another month of training. And then all of our pilots, no matter how long they've been there, come back every month for training in the simulators. And so when you're as big as we are, the facility runs 362 days a year, 20 hours a day. The other four hours of the day are for maintenance of the simulators.

Warner: Basically, an around-the-clock operation. That is, you have people training in the middle of the night. What are the economic impacts for Metro Denver when a pilot, presumably based elsewhere, comes in to train?

Kirby: The far bigger economic impact is just the impact of having the hub here and driving economic activity, causing businesses to want to locate here, bringing tourists here. I don't know how big the impact is, but it's pretty sizable because we have probably 7-800 pilots at that facility at any given time. Most of them are from somewhere else, so they're staying in local hotels, they're spending on local goods and services. It's like having another 7-800 tourists visiting every single day.

Warner: And then you used this word hub. There's no doubt that Denver is a hub for United. Is that an investment that you see growing? So we've talked about training, but let's focus on flights.

Kirby: So yes, the Denver hub does really, really well for us. It's amazing when I first got to United, somebody had a deck about closing the Denver hub. Wall Street was pressuring United to do that. Fortunately, we didn't.

Warner: This is a decade ago that you joined the airline, right?

Kirby: Yeah. And so it wasn't that many years ago that people were talking about it at least. And it was a little over 300 flights a day. I think it’s 560 this summer. We're on the way to growing it to 700. I don't remember if it had any long-haul international destinations, but now we have many. We just added Paris. So it's a growing, successful hub. It does well for us, and it's really a big contributor to the local community as well.

Warner: A previous head of the airport helped me understand that, unlike many of the coastal airports, Los Angeles, the airports in New York, there's room here to grow. There's room to add gates. There's room to add flights, and that's not true at an LAX or a Kennedy.

Kirby: That's true. Some airports in LA, Kennedy, San Francisco, Chicago, all examples of constrained airports

Warner: What was the talk ten years ago that United might abandon Denver?

Kirby: Well, United was sort of down financially. Of ten airlines in the US, it was number nine out of ten. In customer metrics, it was at the bottom. It was a tough time, and we turned it around. People have turned it around, and there was always massive untapped potential at United. I remember when I first came to United, one of the Wall Street analysts named Mike Lindenberg told me he remembered 20 years earlier in my career or 15 years earlier in my career, I'd been at a conference with investors at the time I was kind of young, but little America West Airlines, but people thought young and up-and-comer. Someone asked me what airline I would like to go to if I could pick any airline in the world, and I said United. I didn't remember the story, and they asked why, and I said, ‘Well, it's the most potential. It's just untapped. I don't know why they don't realize the potential, but there's this huge potential there.’ So at least I had a vision for what United could be long ago, and we realized it now. But one of the things that has been expected but has been much bigger than I appreciated was the power of pride potential with employees that they wanted to be on the winning team. And once we started winning, what they were going to do to really make the airline great — that's the secret sauce to making the airline great — is our people. We're in the people business; we're in the service business. And when our people are proud of the airline and believe in the future, they do great things for customers. I knew that they were great people, but because I'd never seen it in action, I didn't fully appreciate how powerful that was going to be, but that's just additional rocket fuel for United.

Warner: I think what you told folks at the Denver Metro Chamber of Commerce annual gathering is that everything emanates from that employee contentment, that if you focus there, the details fall into place. Speaking of employees, I think United was on track to hire 1300 people in Denver this year. Is that still true?

Kirby: I don't know the exact number, but that's certainly directionally correct.

Warner: And what are those jobs?

Kirby: So they're across the board. People that work at the airport, that work in the business office or that are customer service agents, that are flight attendants, that are pilots. A lot of them are at the training center, people that are support staff for the training center. So it's really kind of across the board. But one of the great things about United, one of the things I'm proud of at United, is we don't just create jobs; we create careers. Our pilots make well into the six figures, but even a flight attendant or a gate agent or a technician, certainly with overtime, once they get 12 years, get to the top of the seniority scale, many of them make six-figure incomes.

Warner: That's about retention.

Kirby: Well, it's good for retention. We have extremely low turnover. After the first year, something like 1 or 2%. It's extremely low turnover. But it also makes me proud because I think one of the things that has happened in our country in the last 40, 50 years is a disappearance, hollowing out of the middle class and that there aren't many places that you can go work, support your family, own a home, send your kids to college someday.

Warner: We hear constantly about the housing crunch here and the affordability crisis.

Kirby: Although I think I've watched the numbers, I think the housing numbers have gotten better here in the last few years.

Warner: You mentioned the new service to Paris from Denver starting May 2027. Air France had been schlepping people from Denver to Paris. Do you wait for other carriers to test out a route and then go in and try to put them out of business?

Kirby: No. In fact, we started Denver to Paris later than we would've because there was another carrier on the route. So we probably would've done Paris before Rome had Air France not been here, but we did Rome first and now we're doing Paris.

Warner: And do you hope to coexist along Air France or is it a win if they stop?

Kirby: I think Air France is going to struggle, but airlines tend to not cancel flights. There tends to be a lot of ego involved in where they fly. So I'd be surprised if they pull out, but I'm almost certain that they will lose money. I think they were losing money before, but I think they'll almost for sure lose money now because most of the customers are US citizens going overseas and they're going to, one, I think United's better, but they're going to be biased to fly on United.

Warner: You recently predicted that American Airlines, your former airline, will abandon Chicago as a hub. I wonder if you hope for the same hegemony in Denver.

Kirby: Yeah. Frontier, it's hard for Frontier here in Denver. There's a niche I think that can work for Frontier, and they have a chance now that Spirit went out of business to fill that niche. But trying to compete head-to-head, toe to toe with Delta or United isn't going to work.

And by the way, I think Southwest — I have a lot of respect for Southwest. I like Bob Jordan, what the changes they've made, they've executed close to flawlessly. They've done a great job, but it's hard for them to compete. It used to be if you're a customer in Denver, for some customers at least, Southwest had a unique proposition that you liked better than United. There's now nothing unique about Southwest.

Warner: Seating arrangements changed, of course.

Kirby: Yeah. And there's a lot of things that are similar and same. They do a lot of things well, but there's a lot of things that United does that Southwest doesn't even do. If you want lounges or first class or international flights, a lot of things that we do that they don't even do. So if you're a frequent traveler, you wind up migrating to United. And the numbers are approximately, in 2019, Southwest had six points of higher market share with local Denver customers than United. And I think by the first quarter of this year, we're up to a 16-point advantage. So a 22-point market share swing. And so some of the changes for Southwest, they're I think going to be good for Southwest financially. It's going to make it harder for them to be competitive in Atlanta against Delta or in Denver against United, but it's going to make them way more successful in Kansas City and Austin and San Diego. And honestly, I think their future is to be the number one airline in the number 15 to number 50 cities that aren't hubs for one of the big airlines and really be number one there while the hub carriers drive hub economics and fly to more destinations. And that's my own view of what ultimately happens.

Warner: Reading through United's latest annual report, a few things stood out. First is the promise of sustainable aviation fuel to meet climate goals. Those are your own goals and also the countries in which you operate. What to you is the most promising source of those fuels? And to what extent are we flying already on sustainable fuel?

Kirby: It's low today, sustainable aviation fuel (SAF). I think it's important, all the way back to, I got interested in climate change, as we called it then, when I was a cadet at the Air Force Academy and the science is fascinating. And I can remember reading in the ‘80s, the forecasts were there's going to be less snow on the Western Slope and the Colorado River's going to go dry. We all act surprised that Lake Powell and Lake Mead are at all-time lows. So I think it's really important to do. And United is doing more than any airline around the world to push the edges for sustainable aviation fuel, but it requires government support to make it successful.

Warner: Are you getting that support from this government?

Kirby: The Inflation Reduction Act had some good stuff in it that was a good start, but it was all short-term and we need longer-term incentives. And at its core, think of what we did for solar. If you went back 25 years ago and read the literature, solar was impossible to ever make work because it was too expensive. And I just finished reading the latest Scientific American and it again pointed out solar is now the cheapest form of energy to make around the world. And that's not always on, which is a separate set of problems, but it's the cheapest form to make because there were great government incentives that drove investment to drive efficiency and drive down the cost curve. And once you drive down the cost curve, you don't have to have those incentives, but the incentives built the industry and we have to do the same thing for sustainable aviation fuel. It's the only way it's going to work.

Warner: And is it corn?: What is it? Woody biomass, corn stalk? Algae?

Kirby: That’s one of the ways. There's a bunch of things that you could do. I think algae's not working. It's one of those promises. Algae's sort of like fusion. It just sounded attractive, and it's 10 to 20 years away, and it was 10 to 20 years away 30 years ago and it's still 10 to 20 years away. Algae, we've just never been able to make work.

Warner: And the annual report does mention electric planes as well.

Kirby: Yeah. The electric craft, that's going to be niche. The energy density of batteries is just not high enough to fly even a medium-sized airplane to fly to Kansas City. We might fly a little airplane from here to Breckenridge or something.

But corn soybean is one of the potentials for SAF. And actually, I think it does have broad bipartisan support because one of the rare things like on the left, people are worried about climate change, and on the right, all the states starting here, going several hundred miles to the West that produce corn and soybean are mostly going biodiesel, renewable diesel and ethanol. And that's going to become stranded goods someday because road transport is going to electrify and as it electrifies, what do you do with those stranded assets? The most logical thing, we produce 17 billion gallons today, is to use those existing assets to produce sustainable aviation fuel. I think that's probably the most promising and most likely path, largely because it works; we know it works, the infrastructure exists and there's bipartisan, as close to bipartisan as we can get this day and age.

Warner: But I don't hear you saying that there is that current government investment continuing at least beyond the Inflation Reduction Act under Biden for sustainable aviation fuel.

Kirby: Look, I wouldn't even say it's necessarily even under Biden. That was a good starting point. But even there, and I worked on that legislation, I was proud of that legislation. It was temporary, so it was never going to be enough on its own. It was a starting point, but we haven't done much more since then. And around the globe, nobody's in Europe; they're going the wrong direction compared to what we're doing here.

They're trying to use sticks instead of carrots. Carrots work so much better, like mandating that airlines buy SAF. All that's going to happen is we're going to make it in the United States, we're going to burn carbon to put it on a ship and send it to Europe, and it drives a perverse negative incentive. The sticks drive a negative incentive: that the few people that produce SAF want to charge you an arm and a leg for it because they're the only ones that have it and they have zero incentive to be more efficient and drive down the cost. They, in fact, have negative incentive. They want things to stay expensive, and that's where they make the highest profit margins. So you just drive bad behavior.

Warner: The idea being that some of the mandates are preceding the availability of this fuel, the broad availability and the affordability of it. Well, speaking of affordability, where do you see ticket prices headed?

Kirby: Air travel remains an incredible value. Airfares, they've gone up this year, but even with that, they're still 13% below where they were in real terms compared to 2019. They're about 50% lower than they were 25, 30 years ago. Air travel's an incredible bargain. You fly to Disneyworld, sometimes you're oftentimes, especially if you're on the East Coast, your Uber costs more than your air ticket. One night at the hotel is a lot more than your air ticket. It just got out of whack, the travel portion of the travel pie, and it's going back to a more normalized level. I think they're going to still go up. You look this year, you had one airline completely go out of business. Spirit. You have four of eight US airlines that are — actually, if you include the two that are private — six out of 10 US airlines this year are probably going to lose money. That's not sustainable. The airlines are not charging as much as it costs to fly.

Warner: Is that a post-COVID correction?

Kirby: Yeah. So what really happened is this collapse of airfares during COVID, and we're really recovering from that.

Warner: United has a relationship with Boom Aerospace, which actually moved out of Colorado. Boom wants to see the return of supersonic flight. Is that a pipe dream?

Kirby: I don't think so. It's not a layup. It's not done. I probably wouldn't have said it, but I thought a few years ago that it was a half-court shot. So they've done a lot, and it's now a jumper from the top of the key. It's not even a three-pointer anymore. I think they got a good shot.

Warner: The federal government seems willing to relax some of the rules around supersonic flight over the country. Are you close to buying these things?

Kirby: Well, we've got an order for them. It's contingent. They got to build them, but it's far enough away. It's not today's real issue. It's far enough away, I think, inside of 10 years. If they're going to get it done, it'll be inside of 10 years.

Warner: Okay. I mean, the fuel burn is the big question, right?

Kirby: Well, yes and no. I mean, as you get more SAF, I don't think the fuel burn is going to be really the biggest question. The question is going to be, can you economically build the airplane? Can you get enough range on it to have enough markets that the airplane can work for customers? There's enough demand for enough airplanes that you can build enough to cover the fixed cost of developing it.

Warner: You did mention AI on stage earlier, again, in front of folks at the Denver Metro Chamber of Commerce. And you said there are some crazy uses for AI and there's some decent ones. Where are United passengers seeing good uses of AI and are they replacing employees?

Kirby: So I'll just talk broadly about it. One, I think what most people are using it for right now is just dumb. Use it to summarize my day. Can't you read your calendar? You need another app to help you? We already have a calendar. Summarize documents. What AI is designed to do is give you the consensus, the milquetoast average consensus. I read for three hours a day, and everything interesting that I learned is in between the lines. It's the little things. It's never going to be in the summary. And if you want to be average and you don't ever want to do anything that's different than anyone else, by all means use AI summaries. All the value that gets created, if you're going to do anything big, you've got to figure out something that nobody else knows and figure out where the consensus is wrong. And AI cannot do that for you. It is mathematically designed to not do that.

I also am not apocalyptic about outsourcing jobs. There's going to be some things that are more efficient, yes. But if all we're going to use it for is to do things that humans already do with fewer people, we have wasted trillions of dollars because we're never getting a payback on the trillions that are being spent on AI to do that. To me, the promise of AI is it can do things pretty quickly and easily that were impossible or impractical before. And that's what we're primarily using it for at United.

Warner: A lot of that is channeled through the app, right?

Kirby: Yeah. Within the past week, we rolled out a new feature in the app that is, if there's a flight delay or potential for a delay, like the weather, we will not just tell you there's weather; we'll say, 'Here are some other options if you want to go at a different time of day.’ And by the way, here are places where you can book a confirmed seat or you can stand by for this flight. Here's how many people are ahead of you. Here are your chances of making it.

Warner: It gives me options instead of just information that's going to make me bang my head against the wall?

Kirby: Exactly. And that's exactly what we're trying to do. We're going to even get it to where it will say, ‘Lots of thunderstorms in Denver during the summer. And the forecast for today is at four o'clock: there's 40% chance of thunderstorms that might impact your flight. Here's some options before, here's some options after. There's only a 5% chance if you take this flight.’ You may not be able to, but it will give you options. And AI makes it possible to; it's really powerful for programming, makes it possible to do stuff like that. And there's a class of problems that it's great at solving. One of them that we've experimented with here in Denver — we'd have to get the FAA to do it, but we've run, when there's thunderstorms in the summer, the FAA just closes huge swaths of airspace because they don't know where it's going to go. But we have this amazing database of years of thunderstorms in history. And so we can use that database to more accurately forecast what part of the airspace should close and what part can stay open instead of just manually closing huge swaths of the airspace. And we think that doing that, like we've already run it in real-world experience, we could cut delays by 50% when there's a thunderstorm here. Now that we can't quite use yet because the FAA has to ingest it, but it shows you the power. Cutting delays when there's a thunderstorm by 50% is hugely powerful for customers. So I'm exclusive almost, pretty much I at least am, exclusively focused on what are the things that we can do with AI to make travel better for customers that we could not do before.

Warner: This was fascinating. In the annual report, there is a specific mention of social media and how lethal a viral post can be from a disgruntled passenger. I mean, that can move stock markets. Is that something you can prepare for or is that something you merely blunt after the fact? I don't imagine 10 years ago social media even came up in an annual report.

Kirby: Look, we carry 600,000 people a day. Stuff is going to happen. One, if you create an airline that our employees are proud of and they're doing a great job, you're going to have a lot less of that happen. Most of the incidents that we have on airplanes now are passenger-to-passenger, something that's happening with a passenger. We don't even have many of those. There's a lot of news about — don't even talk about United, about other airlines and stuff happening on airplanes. We carry three million people a day as an industry here in the U.S. every day and it's pretty rare that stuff happens. If you put three million people in a bar in a restaurant, a lot more is going to happen there. So the rate is really low, but it gets high publicity.

But one, creating a great airline is going to reduce the probability that's happened, but also creating a culture where we empower people to do the right thing and take care of customers. The chances get a lot smaller, and then we do a pretty good job, I think. We have a great social media team. They're completely empowered. Actually, I was texting back or emailing back and forth with the head of our social media team this morning because a blogger wrote an article about how great United is social media and I was telling her you guys are awesome and she just told me a story. She's like, 'I talked to people at other companies that do this, and they're so jealous of United because they all have, before they can respond to something, all kinds of people have to sign off on doing so, which means they never say anything or if they do. It's total milquetoast, nothing. And our people are empowered. And look, sometimes they make a mistake, but who cares? That's the world. And they're empowered, and they react with humor. We try to hire people that are good at humor, and they do a great job.

Warner: And the mistake is not making a mistake is something you told recently to the graduates at the Air Force Academy.

Kirby: The biggest mistake most people make in their career is never making a big mistake. They never do anything. They're so afraid of taking a risk, they never do anything.

ASTM International, eine Organisation zur Entwicklung technischer Standards und Prüfverfahren, hat Methanol als zulässigen Rohstoff für den Alcohol-to-Jet-Herstellungspfad anerkannt.
Die Entwicklung nachhaltiger Flugkraftstoffe (Sustainable Aviation Fuels, SAF) hat nun einen wichtigen Meilenstein erreicht: Nach erfolgreicher Qualifizierung durch die internationale Standardisierungsorganisation ASTM wurde Methanol als zulässiger Rohstoff für den Alcohol-to-Jet-Herstellungspfad anerkannt.
