text:
ASTM International, eine Organisation zur Entwicklung technischer Standards und Prüfverfahren, hat Methanol als zulässigen Rohstoff für den Alcohol-to-Jet-Herstellungspfad anerkannt. Bei diesem Verfahren werden Alkohole chemisch in Flugkraftstoffkomponenten umgewandelt.

Die weltweit mehr als 23.000 Großflugzeuge verbrauchen jährlich rund 350 Milliarden Liter Treibstoff und emittieren etwa 3 Prozent der menschgemachten CO2-Emissionen. Insbesondere für Langstreckenflüge über 4.000 km gibt es keine Alternative zu flüssigen Kraftstoffen, da nur diese eine ausreichend hohe Energiedichte bereitstellen.

Die Entwicklung nachhaltiger Flugkraftstoffe (Sustainable Aviation Fuels, SAF) hat nun einen wichtigen Meilenstein erreicht: Nach erfolgreicher Qualifizierung durch die internationale Standardisierungsorganisation ASTM wurde Methanol als zulässiger Rohstoff für den Alcohol-to-Jet-Herstellungspfad anerkannt.

Damit können künftig Methanol-to-Jet-Blendingkomponenten hergestellt und mit mindestens 50 Volumenprozent konventionellem Kerosin zu einem »Drop-in«-Kraftstoff gemischt werden - vollständig kompatibel und ohne Änderungen an Flugzeugen, Triebwerken oder der bestehenden Infrastruktur einsetzbar.

Für das vom Bundesministerium für Verkehr geförderte Verbundprojekt »SAFari« markiert diese Entscheidung einen bedeutenden Meilenstein. Sie wurde am 30. Juli 2026 mit der Überarbeitung der internationalen Spezifikation ASTM D7566 Annex 5 veröffentlicht. Das Projekt verfolgt das Ziel, einen effizienten Herstellungsprozess für nachhaltigen Flugkraftstoff auf Basis von Methanol zu entwickeln und damit einen weiteren technologischen Baustein für die Defossilisierung der Luftfahrt bereitzustellen.

Während der mehrjährigen Arbeiten begleiteten die Projektpartner den ASTM-Qualifizierungsprozess als Mitglieder der Task Force Methanol-to-Jet eng. Die Erkenntnisse aus dem Evaluierungsprozess konnten so frühzeitig in die Projektarbeiten einfließen und bei der Entwicklung des Herstellungsverfahrens berücksichtigt werden. Hierbei war die frühzeitige Bewertung der Kraftstoffqualität ein wichtiger Indikator für den Projekterfolg. Da in dieser Entwicklungsphase zunächst nur geringe Kraftstoffmengen verfügbar waren, kam das am DLR-Institut für Verbrennungstechnik entwickelte Prescreening-Verfahren zum Einsatz. Es ermöglicht eine umfassende Bewertung der Kraftstoffqualität bereits mit kleinen Probenmengen und liefert eine frühzeitige Einschätzung, ob ein Kraftstoff die Anforderungen der ASTM-Spezifikation erfüllt. Die Ergebnisse flossen unmittelbar in die Prozess- und Katalysatorentwicklung ein und trugen dazu bei, die im Projekt entwickelten Methanol-to-Jet-(MTJ)-Blendingkomponenten gezielt auf die zu erwartenden internationalen Spezifikationsanforderungen auszurichten.

Nachhaltiges Methanol als Basis für neuen Flugkraftstoff

Die SAF-Herstellung auf Basis von MTJ-Technologien nutzt nachhaltiges Methanol aus biogenen Quellen oder gewonnen aus Wasserstoff und abgeschiedenem CO₂. In der Methanol-to-Olefins-Synthese (MTO) wird dieses Methanol in kurzkettige Olefine umgewandelt, wobei Wasser als Nebenprodukt den Sauerstoff aus dem Prozess entfernt. Die kurzkettigen Olefine werden anschließend in einer Oligomerisierung zu langkettigen Olefinen zusammengeführt, sodass ein bei Raumtemperatur flüssiges Produktgemisch entsteht. Durch Hydrierung mit Wasserstoff werden die Olefine in stabile Paraffine umgewandelt. Das Ergebnis ist ein Kraftstoffgemisch, das die den hohen Anforderungen der Luftfahrt erfüllt.

»Im SAFari-Projekt entwickeln wir gemeinsam mit unseren Partnern ein innovatives Verfahren, das durch maßgeschneiderte Katalysatoren und prozessinterne Rückführungen von Stoffströmen und Wärme eine kohlenstoffbasierte SAF-Ausbeute von über 85 Gewichtsprozent anstrebt. Mit dem erfolgreichen Abschluss des ASTM-Qualifizierungsverfahrens ist nun eine der größten Hürden für die Demonstration und Skalierung überwunden«, erklärt Dr. Elias Frei, Bereichsleiter Wasserstofftechnologien am Fraunhofer ISE.

»Nach der erfolgreichen ASTM-Qualifizierung richtet sich der Fokus des Projekts nun auf die weitere Optimierung und Skalierung des Herstellungsprozesses«, blickt Dr. Achim Schaadt, Abteilungsleiter Nachhaltige Syntheseprodukte, nach vorn. »Ziel ist es, größere Kraftstoffmengen bereitzustellen, um weiterführende Untersuchungen und Demonstrationen durchzuführen und damit den Weg für eine industrielle Umsetzung von Methanol-basiertem Sustainable Aviation Fuel zu ebnen«, ergänzt Dr. Franz Mantei, Projektleiter des SAFari-Projekts. Das Marktpotenzial für diese Technologie ist dabei enorm: Allein für den europäischen Flugverkehr ergeben sich durch die vorgegebenen Quoten rund 40 Mio. t im Jahr 2050.

Zum Konsortium des Projekts SAFari („Sustainable Aviation Fuels based on Advanced Reaction and Process Intensification“) gehören neben dem Fraunhofer ISE die ASG Analytik-Service AG, die BP Europa SE, die Clariant Produkte (Deutschland) GmbH, das Deutsche Zentrum für Luft- und Raumfahrt e.V. (DLR), die Technip Energies France S.A.S sowie die Südzucker AG, der Bundesverband der Deutschen Luftverkehrswirtschaft e.V. (BDL) und die Airbus Helicopters Deutschland GmbH. Damit bildet das Konsortium die gesamte Wertschöpfungskette ab. Das SAFari-Projekt wird seit dem 1. Dezember 2022 vom Bundesministerium für Verkehr (BMV) für die Dauer von sechs Jahren gefördert.

title: Sustainable Aviation Fuel Levies - Clean the Sky
description:
Singapore delayed its SAF Levy for departing cargo flights by one year, giving the freight industry more time to build a workable collection system, while its passenger levy proceeds as planned starting in January 2027.
The delay reflects the added complexity of cargo transactions, which involve airlines, freight forwarders, shippers and varied commercial arrangements, compared with passenger ticketing.
The levy funds Singapore's broader Sustainable Air Hub Blueprint, which aims for a 20% reduction in domestic aviation emissions by 2030 and net-zero aviation emissions by 2050.
Proceeds will go to a dedicated fund administered by Singapore Sustainable Aviation Fuel Company, which will procure and allocate sustainable aviation fuel.
Singapore's phased rollout provides a valuable case study for other governments on how centralized levy systems can effectively translate long-term climate goals into practical procurement frameworks.

text:
By Anne Cosgrove

From the July / August 2026 Issue

Minnesota continues to distinguish itself offering businesses a blend of innovation, workforce quality, advanced manufacturing, and corporate stability. Home to 17 Fortune 500 headquarters and one of the nation’s deepest concentrations of medical technology, food processing, and advanced manufacturing companies, Minnesota offers businesses a mature ecosystem built around research, skilled labor, and long-term investment.

During 2025, the state continued attracting expansion projects while reinforcing its position as a national leader in life sciences, clean technology, and precision manufacturing. Governor Tim Walz has maintained an economic development strategy centered on workforce development, business expansion, and strategic public-private partnerships, while emphasizing Minnesota’s strengths in innovation and quality of life.

For site selectors evaluating locations where workforce capability and innovation outweigh low-cost operating models, Minnesota continues to present a compelling value proposition.

Rather than relying on a single dominant industry for economic growth, the state has developed globally competitive clusters in medical technology, life sciences, food and agriculture, advanced manufacturing, financial services, aerospace, and clean energy.

For the past several years, Minnesota has been building a regional ecosystem capable of producing, delivering and using sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) at commercial scale. With the recent completion of a new blending facility at Flint Hills Resources’ Pine Bend Refinery, sustainable aviation fuel can now be blended, certified and delivered directly to Minneapolis-Saint Paul International Airport (MSP) in commercial volumes. The facility adds one of the final pieces of infrastructure needed to launch Minnesota’s SAF economy.

“This is the moment Minnesota’s SAF economy begins,” said Peter Frosch, President and CEO of the GREATER MSP Partnership. “Three years of collaboration among business, government, universities and environmental organizations has resulted in entirely new infrastructure that will serve Minnesota—and the world—for decades to come.”

Minnesota’s public, private and academic sectors came together to intentionally build this ecosystem—from policy and feedstocks to production, infrastructure and market demand. That work has included bipartisan state policies, demonstration flights, partnerships with farmers and fuel producers, investment in research, and the creation of the nation’s first regional SAF hub. The new blending facility is the connective tissue that allows those pieces to function as a complete value chain.

North Wind Aerospace

In January, St. Paul-based North Wind announced it is investing $1.1 billion to build an aerospace and hypersonic research and testing complex in Rosemount. The project is a public-private partnership and investment in Minnesota’s innovation economy while significantly expanding the nation’s limited capacity for advanced high-speed aerospace testing.

The Minnesota Aerospace Complex will serve commercial and government customers nationwide, providing independent, high-fidelity ground testing across a full spectrum of flight: subsonic, transonic, supersonic, and hypersonic. Designed to support the development of next-generation aircraft, propulsion systems, sensors, and aerospace technologies, the complex fills a critical national infrastructure gap while anchoring this capability in Minnesota.

Developed and operated by North Wind, the complex builds on the company’s Minnesota roots and international reputation for technical excellence. North Wind is a nationally recognized aerospace engineering firm whose clients include NASA, major aerospace companies, the U.S. Department of Energy, and the U.S. Department of Defense.

“The North Wind investment will be the foundation of a new high-tech industry in Minnesota. This project is a step toward realizing our vision for our next economy, which creates inclusive opportunity for Minnesotans by solving the hardest, most important challenges for the nation and the world,” said Frosch.

A defining element of the Aerospace Complex is its partnership with the University of Minnesota, including colocation of the University’s Computational Hypersonics Research Laboratory.

The Aerospace Complex also represents a significant land redevelopment transformation for the region. The project will kickstart environmental cleanup and redevelopment of a long-idle, contaminated 60-acre site at UMore Park.

Polar Semiconductor Expands In Minnesota

One of Minnesota’s most significant advanced manufacturing investments continues to be Polar Semiconductor’s expansion in Bloomington. The company is investing approximately $525 million to expand production of specialty semiconductor chips used in automotive, aerospace, medical, and industrial applications. The project is expected to retain roughly 700 existing jobs while creating more than 160 new high-skilled positions over time.

The expansion combines federal CHIPS Act funding with support from the State of Minnesota, including DEED assistance through the Minnesota Investment Fund and other workforce development programs.

Polar Semiconductor CEO Surya Iyer said the expansion would allow the company to meet growing demand for U.S.-based semiconductor manufacturing while supporting resilient domestic supply chains.

Workforce Focus

Governor Tim Walz’s administration has continued emphasizing workforce investment, innovation, and support for business expansion while promoting Minnesota as a destination for advanced manufacturing and technology.

Record activity through the state’s Job Creation Fund and Minnesota Investment Fund, combined with major investments such as Polar Semiconductor’s expansion, illustrates an economic development strategy focused on strengthening existing industry clusters while attracting new opportunities.

title: Cathay's 80 years of trailblazing travel
description:
On 24 September 1946, just one day after Cathay Pacific Airways was registered in Hong Kong for HK$2, we operated our first flight from Sydney to Hong Kong.
The following morning, CX889 “Polar One” landed at the newly opened Hong Kong International Airport (HKIA) at Chek Lap Kok.
Today, Cathay Cargo carries about 1.7 million tonnes of cargo annually.
As Cathay has evolved into a leading travel lifestyle brand, we’ve diversified the ways we connect to our customers.
“Cathay’s story is inseparable from Hong Kong, from our deep connections to the Chinese Mainland and from our place in the wider world.
text:
Cathay's story began in 1946 with a single converted cargo plane, two visionary pilots and an ambition to connect people across Asia Pacific. Eight decades later, that pioneering spirit still guides us, carrying us from our earliest days to become one of our customers’ most loved service brands.

In the aftermath of the Second World War, our co-founders, former Air Force pilots Roy Farrell and Sydney de Kantzow, set out to build something remarkable, starting with a mission to fly goods from Australia to Shanghai. On 24 September 1946, just one day after Cathay Pacific Airways was registered in Hong Kong for HK$2, we operated our first flight from Sydney to Hong Kong. Our fleet then consisted of a single aircraft: a converted Douglas DC-3 affectionately known as “Betsy”.

The years that followed saw us spread our wings. In the 1960s, our Convair 880 jetliners extended our network across Asia to destinations including Seoul and Kota Kinabalu. The jet age transformed flying, making air travel faster and more accessible: on 19 October 1964, we welcomed our millionth passenger aboard a flight from Singapore to Bangkok.

“Since our earliest days, Cathay has helped open new horizons for people, businesses and communities,” says Cathay Group CEO Ronald Lam. “That purpose has defined our first 80 years, and it continues to guide us today.”

Another defining chapter began in 1979 with the arrival of our first Boeing 747. The jumbo jet extended our reach beyond the region and laid the foundations for a truly global network. The following year, we launched our first service to London.

Throughout the 1980s, generations of Hong Kong people looked skyward as our Boeing 747s, painted in their iconic green-and-white-striped “lettuce leaf sandwich” liveries, swept low over Kowloon on their approach to Kai Tak – enduring symbols of a city reaching out to the world. The ’80s brought the expansion of passenger services to the Chinese Mainland, starting with Shanghai in 1980. In 1983, we became the first airline in Asia to offer First class, Business class and Economy cabins on the same aircraft, setting new benchmarks for service. Three years later, as we marked our 40th anniversary, we became the first company to list on Hong Kong’s unified stock exchange. As our fleet and route map expanded, so did our understanding of our passengers’ needs.

In 1991, we were the first airline to introduce live radio on board, bringing music and news directly to passengers in flight. Seatback entertainment soon followed, arriving in First class in 1992 before extending across every cabin by 1996.

The end of the Kai Tak era marked another unforgettable moment. On 5 July 1998, CX251 to London Heathrow became the last flight to depart the legendary airport. The following morning, CX889 “Polar One” landed at the newly opened Hong Kong International Airport (HKIA) at Chek Lap Kok. It was the first non-stop passenger service from New York to Hong Kong and the longest non-stop commercial flight in operation at the time.

In the same year, we took delivery of our first Boeing 777-300, an aircraft that would form the backbone of our long-haul fleet. The arrival of the Airbus A350 in 2016 ushered in a new era of efficiency and comfort. More recently, the introduction of new cabin products on selected Boeing 777-300ER aircraft has marked another chapter in the continual evolution of the passenger experience, with refreshed Business, Premium Economy and Economy designs elevating every journey.

While our first freighters began operations in 1976, cargo became an even more important pillar of our business in the 2000s. The HK$5.9 billion Cathay Cargo Terminal entered full operation in 2013 as one of the world’s largest and most advanced air cargo facilities, cementing Hong Kong as a leading international air freight hub. Today, Cathay Cargo carries about 1.7 million tonnes of cargo annually.

Throughout our journey, we’ve continued to push boundaries. In April 2025, we set a record for our longest route with the launch of Dallas-Fort Worth. Our network now spans more than 100 destinations worldwide, strengthened by recently launched routes to Urumqi, Munich and Seattle, with Almaty joining the network in 2027.

Our latest investments extend beyond our route network. New Airbus A321neo aircraft are bringing enhanced comfort and entertainment for a more refined travel experience, while our acclaimed Aria Suite in Business class and refreshed Premium Economy and Economy cabins on selected Boeing 777-300ER aircraft are setting new standards for long-haul flying. Soon, our refreshed Economy cabins and Aria Studio in Business on board our Airbus A330-300 fleet will mark the next chapter in regional travel.

As Cathay has evolved into a leading travel lifestyle brand, we’ve diversified the ways we connect to our customers. From digital innovations that make every stage of a journey more seamless to deeper integration with transport links across the Greater Bay Area, we’re creating a more connected travel ecosystem. Beyond flying, Cathay now offers a growing range of lifestyle, dining, shopping and wellness experiences that enrich everyday life. At the same time, we remain committed to building a more sustainable future for aviation through investments in newer, more fuel-efficient aircraft, measures to reduce emissions across our operations and accelerating the adoption of Sustainable Aviation Fuel. Through these efforts, we aim to create lasting value for our customers, our home city and the communities we serve.

“As we celebrate 80 Years Together, we do so with gratitude for everyone who’s been part of our journey,” says Lam. “Cathay’s story is inseparable from Hong Kong, from our deep connections to the Chinese Mainland and from our place in the wider world. Our responsibility now is to honour that legacy by building on it, so future generations can continue to discover the joy of travel.”

title: Canada extends federal fuel excise tax relief on aviation fuels - Skies Mag

title: The entrepreneur who failed at retirement and turned to waste - UAE - EnterpriseAM
description:
Her return to business eventually led her somewhere she never expected: the waste industry.
I had my own dance school, did some television work, and eventually ran a large export and retail business.
Our UK business takes municipal solid waste — the waste you and I produce every day — and converts it into electricity through gasification.
We process around 250k tons of waste annually and generate roughly 26-28 MW of power.
Our second vertical is sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).
text:
After spending much of her career building and running businesses across retail, manufacturing, and exports, Veena Munganahalli (LinkedIn) was set to retire in 2016. Her return to business eventually led her somewhere she never expected: the waste industry. Alongside her co-founder and husband, she launched Sencirc, an Abu Dhabi-based holding company investing in a portfolio that spans energy-from-waste, sustainable aviation fuel, and, soon, compressed biogas — all built around a simple prospect: waste has value, provided you can find a commercially viable way to unlock it.

Each week, My Morning Routine looks at how a successful member of the community starts their day — and then throws in a couple of business questions just for fun. This week, we spoke with Munganahalli about accidentally becoming a waste-to-value entrepreneur. Edited excerpts from our conversation:

EnterpriseAM: Take us back to the beginning. Why go into the waste-to-value business?

Veena Munganahalli (VM): I've been an entrepreneur since I was 12. I had my own dance school, did some television work, and eventually ran a large export and retail business. I exited all of that around 2016 because I thought, ‘I'm done for life.’ I wanted to be a stay-at-home mom and do all the things I thought I had missed out on. Turns out, I suck at it. So, I started mentoring women entrepreneurs and investing in impact startups.

Around 2021, my husband and I started thinking about what we wanted to do with the next 20 years of our lives. We had the opportunity to acquire a sustainable energy business in the UK, and we spent about 18 months researching the industry before deciding to do it. That's where Sencirc came from. The idea is to create a future that is circularly sensible.

E: What does that actually mean in practice? What does Sencirc do?

VM: We focus on businesses that convert waste into value. Our first vertical is energy from waste. Our UK business takes municipal solid waste — the waste you and I produce every day — and converts it into electricity through gasification. We process around 250k tons of waste annually and generate roughly 26-28 MW of power.

Our second vertical is sustainable aviation fuel (SAF). Aviation has very few options for decarbonization, and the idea is to use waste or carbon that's already circulating rather than extracting more carbon from the ground through fossil fuels. We partnered with Novus Aviation Capital to establish SAF One, and our first project is coming up in Kakinada in southern India. We will use waste oils, including used cooking oil, to produce SAF. The third vertical, which we are preparing to launch, is compressed biogas. It will use agricultural waste, including paddy straw and sugarcane residue, to create gas.

E: What has surprised you most about working in this industry?

VM: It's a heavy industrial business, and there are so many women in leadership and managerial positions. I think women are intrinsically sustainable. We know how to rotate resources. The other thing that has amazed me is how much younger people are buying into the industry. They actively write to us asking for internships and opportunities. You may be doing something today that benefits people hundreds of years from now. There is a huge amount of forethought, and I love that about this industry.

E: What can the UAE do better when it comes to sustainability?

VM: Segregation has to start at the household level. I lived in Switzerland, where the rules around waste were incredibly strict. If your bin wasn't properly closed, you could be fined. The responsibility was on individuals to make sure they were segregating waste properly. We need to start making that part of everyday life. Otherwise, everything goes into the same bin.

E: Tell us about your morning routine. How does your day begin?

VM: I'm very South Indian at heart. I have to have a newspaper and coffee in my hand. I still read at least one newspaper from start to finish while listening to some music. I'm not a morning person, but that's how I start. Because we work across different time zones, my mornings are also for catching up on emails and messages before the day properly begins.

I've never had a to-do list because I think it constrains you. People get stressed because they haven't finished everything on their list, and I hate that feeling. If something is urgent and I'm worried I'll forget it, I send myself a WhatsApp message. That's my to-do list.

E: How does this pace of life compare with your earlier years of running businesses?

VM: My earlier business involved around 40 retail touchpoints. Somebody hadn't opened a store. There was a regulatory problem. A manufacturing issue had come up somewhere. I used to wake up firefighting and go to bed firefighting. Now, we know what we want, we're deliberate about who we hire, and we encourage our teams to make decisions.

E: What is one constant in your day that keeps you grounded?

VM: Apart from the newspaper and coffee, I speak to each of my daughters every single day.

Recently, I've also developed a habit of lighting a lamp every morning. I don't know exactly why I started doing it, but I miss it when I travel. I don't do elaborate routines. I don't meditate or do breathwork because I don't want to create intentions that become stressful to maintain. I like simple things. Maybe I'll buy a random pair of earrings — I collect junk earrings. That's good enough for me.

E: And how do you switch off when work is finally over?

VM: I don't want to go to sleep thinking about the next management book I need to read or some great thing everyone else is doing. I want to sleep in meaninglessness. Give me a comedy, a crime show, or something completely silly. At the end of the day, I have only one thought: I now need to sleep. Fortunately, I sleep like a baby.

Veena's favorites

What she watches: Crime dramas and “brainless” Netflix. Reacher gets a mention.

Best advice she's received: Never start a business alone. Find a co-founder who complements your skills and doesn't simply think exactly like you. A business is a giant. It can eat you up and consume you. You shouldn't be alone on that journey.

The energy transition now spans a wide range of areas, including renewable energy development, marine engineering, microgrids, data centers, sustainability disclosure, transition finance, CCUS, and SAF.

The "2026 Comprehensive Energy Development & Carbon Quest For The Future" was taking place on August 20, bringing together representatives from government, industry, academia and research institutions to focus on energy transition, low-carbon development and the future competitiveness of businesses.[1]

The rapid expansion of AI, the semiconductor industry and data centers is redefining the global competition for energy and net-zero leadership. From reliable low-carbon power and renewable energy development to sustainability disclosure, transition finance and the commercialization of low-carbon technologies, energy and carbon management have evolved from corporate sustainability concerns into core determinants of operational resilience and capital competitiveness.

EnergyOMNI, an energy and net-zero information platform, and RECCESSARY, a new energy and carbon market information platform, jointly hosted the 2nd "2026 Comprehensive Energy Development & Carbon Quest For The Future" Forum (「全能佈局・碳贏未來」論壇) from August 20 to 21. The event brought together government officials, international representatives, energy and technology companies, financial institutions and 3rd-party verification organizations to examine the new wave of transformation challenges facing businesses in the AI era, spanning the entire spectrum from energy supply to capital markets.

EnergyOMNI's founder, Xin-En (Joi) Wu (吳心恩), stated that the company has consistently focused on integrating energy information across various disciplines and platforms. EnergyOMNI conducts independent research on critical issues while providing perspectives that are distinct from those in other media outlets. As EnergyOMNI enters its 4th year, Wu emphasized that the number "4" symbolizes the completeness and stability created by the 4 directions (East, West, North, South) and 4 seasons (which represent the whole year). She further expressed her hope that EnergyOMNI will continue to be a stabilizing force in the industry, fostering connections across sectors and expanding its influence.

RECCESSARY founder, Kung-Hui (Jason) Huang (黃公暉), said the "Comprehensive Energy Development & Carbon Quest For The Future" forum series is committed to bringing together perspectives from different fields. The value of the forum lies not only in discussions of key issues, but also in serving as a platform for facilitating concrete collaboration. Companies that successfully identify partners, generate orders, or close deals through the forum will achieve the forum's most significant and impactful outcome.

Director-General of the Energy Administration, Chih-Wei Wu, delivers remarks at the event.

AI Drives Up Power Demand: Energy Competition Shifts from "Having Power" to "Reliable Low-Carbon Power"

Chih-Wei Wu (吳志偉), Deputy Director General of Energy Administration, MOEA, said green power has become an important determinant of industrial competitiveness. Taiwan is not only a major global supplier of equipment for AI infrastructure, but must also build its own AI infrastructure, meaning demand for green power and pressure on electricity supply will continue to rise. The government will continue promoting offshore wind and solar PV while helping the private sector overcome development barriers through interdepartmental coordination, regulatory improvements and the design of viable business models.

Joel Derbyshire, Director of Trade and Investment at the British Office, said the energy transition and AI revolution are reshaping global industries at the same time. While AI is rapidly driving up electricity demand, it is also further linking energy security, net-zero targets and industrial competitiveness. Against this backdrop, no single perspective is sufficient to support decision-making. Only by integrating policy, technology, capital and industry perspectives can the true risks and opportunities of the transition be fully understood. The UK has extensive experience in offshore wind, smart grids and green finance, while Taiwan has strengths in semiconductors, offshore wind and digital transformation. He expressed hope that closer UK-Taiwan cooperation would jointly enhance energy security, advance net-zero goals and foster next-generation innovation.

Joel Derbyshire, Director of Trade and Investment at the British Office, delivered the opening remarks on Day 1 of the forum.

Chia-Chin Tsai (蔡佳晋), General Manager of Ina Energy (寶晶能源), stated the rapidly increasing power density of AI servers means AI Data Center (AIDC) require more than simply electricity but need "Firm Power." Companies will have to consider capacity, reliability, scalability, carbon intensity and power delivery schedules simultaneously. The timing, location, quality and carbon intensity of energy supplies will also influence site selection for data centers and high-tech industries.

The growing demand for green power driven by AI is also placing greater emphasis on offshore wind's engineering execution capabilities. Kuo-Cheng (Robert) Tseng (曾國正), Chairman of CSBC-DEME Wind Engineering (CDWE), said Taiwan's offshore wind industry is expected to enter a development scale of 2 GW per year, but construction vessels, marine engineering teams, specialized personnel and port infrastructure all face challenges. As Taiwan, Japan, South Korea and Europe compete simultaneously for engineering resources, the government needs to reduce the risk of supply chain and construction-resource bottlenecks through project scheduling and engineering integration.

Head of the European Economic and Trade Office, Christoph Saurenbach, delivers a keynote speech at the event, discussing prospects for Taiwan-EU cooperation in renewable energy and the semiconductor industry.

Kuo-Lun (Kevin) Wu (吳國綸), APAC Director at OEG Renewables, shared the challenges facing Taiwan's offshore wind market in terms of engineering continuity and resource allocation from the perspective of an international marine energy services provider. He asserted that project continuity, policy predictability, and the capacity of vessels, engineering teams, and supply chains to ensure long-term participation are essential for sustaining market competitiveness.

Chun-li Lee (李君禮), Honorary Consultant of ICCT (義大利商會) and moderator of the panel discussion, noted that corporate low-carbon competitiveness depends not only on access to green electricity, but also on whether the engineering, supply chains and infrastructure behind it have the capacity to provide long-term support. As AI-driven electricity demand grows alongside the energy transition, the ability to execute and finance offshore wind, marine engineering and renewable energy projects will directly affect whether low-carbon electricity can be delivered reliably.

Chun-Hsing (Jonas) Yen (顏君行), Manager of Wind Energy and Carbon Service Department at TÜV Rheinland (德國萊因), stated that renewable energy projects involve substantial capital investment, while 3rd-party Technology Due Diligence (TDD) can identify risks related to power generation, equipment reliability, grid connection and O&M. This can improve project bankability and alleviate concerns among banks and investors.

The Day 1 of the forum focuses on the energy transition and evolving energy demand in the AI era, exploring how businesses can develop next-generation energy strategies spanning low-carbon power, energy resilience and electricity demand from AI data centers.

Meanwhile, AIDC energy strategies are shifting from annual total-volume matching under RE100 toward the more stringent standard of "24/7 carbon-free energy matching." Chee-Hoe Fang (馮志豪), Strategic Alliance Business Manager at Shell (殼牌), said that AI data centers must simultaneously address the "Energy Trilemma" of energy security, affordability and environmental sustainability.

Joanna Lean, General Manager of New Business Development at Shell, cited Shell's collaboration with Google in the UK as an example of how companies are beginning to use energy aggregation to bring low-carbon electricity closer to actual consumption periods.

(From left to right) Chun-li Lee, Honorary Consultant of ICCT｜Chia-Chin Tsai, General Manager of Ina Energy｜Robert Tseng, Chairman of CDWE｜Jonas Yen, Manager of Wind Energy and Carbon Service Department at TÜV Rheinland｜Kevin Wu, APAC Director at OEG Renewables

Ya-Jung (Sunny) Lee (李雅蓉), Director of Strategic Marketing in Energy Infrastructure Business Group at Delta Electronics (台達電), said that an increasing number of regions are requiring AIDCs to "Bring Your Own Power," further increasing the importance of microgrids, energy storage and diversified distributed energy resources.

Hsiao-Yang (Gavin) Wang (王孝揚) , Founder and Chairman of ETICA Battery (明曜科技), also expressed that as GPU power consumption rises, 800V high-voltage direct current (HVDC) will become an important direction for next-generation data center power distribution. Integrating HVDC with UPS energy storage and microgrids can reduce conversion losses and enhance energy flexibility.

Tsu-Hua Ai (艾祖華), Honorary Chair of the SEMI Taiwan Smart Energy Storage Committee (SEMI 智慧儲能委員會), said that from a power-system perspective that as the share of renewable energy and AI-driven electricity demand both increase, energy storage and microgrids will play an increasingly important role in stabilizing the power grid. Beyond technological integration, the continued improvement of ancillary-service mechanisms and electricity market structures will also affect the scale of energy storage investment and deployment.

Lily Liao (廖梨嫆), Deputy General Manager, Solar and Commercial & Industrial Products Service Division, TÜV Rheinland, warned that as AIDC technologies advance rapidly, Taiwan's supply chain must simultaneously keep pace with standards including TIA-942, ISO/IEC 22237 and EN 50600, as well as sustainability requirements such as PUE, REF and WUE, in order to reduce market-entry and compliance risks when expanding overseas.

Sammy Su (蘇冬蘭), Head of Sustainability Strategy at TÜV Rheinland and co-moderator of the panel discussion, emphasized that the landscape of competition among AIDC has transformed. It is no longer sufficient to focus solely on computing power and equipment; the ability to establish a robust integrated energy architecture that balances reliability, cost, and resilience is now paramount. As AIDC expand rapidly, companies must proactively integrate energy storage, renewable energy, and backup systems. Furthermore, they must prioritize energy efficiency, cybersecurity, power supply stability, and regulatory compliance within a comprehensive risk management framework. For investors, the critical factor moving forward will be not just the sophistication of technologies, but their quantifiable, verifiable capabilities that can be effectively translated into sustainable investment value.

Day 2 centers on corporate net-zero transition and carbon governance, examining key strategies for building net-zero competitiveness through sustainability disclosures, green finance and low-carbon business models.[2]

Sustainability Shifts from "Commitment" to "Accountability" as Carbon Data Begins to Influence Capital Allocation

While the first day of the forum focused on how companies can secure energy, the focus on the 2nd morning shifted toward how companies can demonstrate that they are genuinely undergoing transformation.

Eugene Chien (簡又新), Chairman of the Taiwan Institute for Sustainable Energy and Ambassador-at-Large, said in his address on the second day of the forum that the global net-zero transition has evolved from a commitment into a competitive race. Companies are no longer facing isolated decarbonization initiatives, but rather systemic challenges involving governance, data, energy, supply chains, finance and technology.

Chien explained the concept of a "comprehensive strategy" through "3 meanings, 5 areas of planning and 3 outcomes." Companies must pursue a comprehensive energy transition, upgrade their capabilities across the board and foster ecosystem-wide collaboration, while simultaneously developing strategies across 5 areas: governance, data, decarbonization, finance and technology. This approach would move sustainability disclosures into business decision-making, shift decarbonization from isolated actions toward long-term transformation capabilities, and ultimately help Taiwan's supply chains become globally trusted low-carbon value chains. He stressed that the key to future competitiveness will not simply be who declares net zero first, but who can truly integrate governance, data, decarbonization, finance and technology to turn decarbonization pressures into drivers of innovation and competitiveness.

Eugene Chien, Chairman of TAISE and Ambassador-at-Large, delivered the opening remarks on the forum's 2nd day

Gennie Yen (嚴德芬), Founder of CSRone (CSRone 永續智庫), said energy and carbon have evolved from areas that could provide companies with a competitive advantage into an unavoidable competitive arena. As carbon costs, electricity risks and capital screening pressures rise simultaneously, companies seeking to outperform cannot focus solely on their own capabilities and conditions. Instead, they must understand broader market and industry developments and fully integrate energy and carbon management into business decision-making.

Chien-Yu Chen (陳建佑), Executive Vice President of CSRone, said global sustainability frameworks are shifting from target-setting toward action and impact measurement. As frameworks including SBTi, the GHG Protocol and ISO standards continue to evolve, carbon data is no longer simply information disclosed in sustainability reports. It will increasingly influence corporate capital allocation, supply chain eligibility and market competitiveness.

Taiwanese listed companies will also gradually align with IFRS S1 and S2. Bryan Lin (林哲仰), Senior Associate Vice President, Sustainability Innovation and Development Department, Nan Shan Life Insurance (南山人壽), said that sustainability information will become a common corporate language used by boards of directors, shareholders, management, analysts and regulators. Companies, however, will also face practical challenges involving data integration, materiality assessment and disclosure timelines.

Sustainability disclosure is becoming increasingly linked to capital markets. Cathy Lee (李介文), Senior Executive Vice President of Deloitte (勤業眾信), indicated that financial policy is shifting from "green finance" toward "transition finance." In the future, even industries with high carbon emissions, like cement and chemicals, may receive financial support if they provide credible transition plans. These plans should include clear timelines, emissions reduction targets, funding sources, and implementation methods. In other words, merely stating a commitment to achieve net-zero emissions is no longer adequate; companies must develop measurable, trackable, and verifiable transition pathways.

The 2nd day also explores low-carbon technologies and business development, covering diverse low-carbon energy sources, CCUS, low-carbon fuels and carbon removal, while examining how decarbonization initiatives can create new opportunities for corporate low-carbon transformation and sustainable development.

Beyond Wind and Solar: The Next Low-Carbon Energy Battle is About Costs and Business Models

As electricity demand increases, corporate energy options are also expanding beyond conventional wind and solar power. The 2nd afternoon of the forum focused on fuel cells, energy efficiency, biogas, CCUS, Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) and carbon credits. The central question is no longer simply whether a technology can reduce emissions, but whether policy, costs and market demand can come together to create sustainable business models.

Cheng-Yen Lao (勞成琰), PhD., Bloom Energy, stated that fuel cells can provide stable power generation at the point of consumption regardless of weather conditions and can operate in island mode, making them a distributed energy option for power-intensive industries such as data centers and semiconductors.

Yi-Kai Wang (王翊愷), General Manager of EcoSoar Energy (續翔節能) Service and VP of Customer Development at Anneal Energy (艾涅爾電力), stressed that "The greenest electricity is the electricity that is saved." Companies should first reduce demand through equipment upgrades, smart controls and energy management before procuring green power.

Yao-Hua Fang (方耀華), General Manager of Universe Circular Technology (宇陽能源), said that biogas can convert agricultural, livestock and organic waste into dispatchable renewable energy, but challenges remain in securing feedstock, coordinating across government agencies and achieving commercial scale.

(From left to right) Jason Huang, Founder of RECCESSARY｜Chun-Te Tso, Vice President of the Taiwan Institute of TIER｜Pei-Ling Lu, Chief Sustainability Officer of STARLUX Airlines｜Hsiang-Yin Wang, Deputy Manager of Sustainability and Carbon Trading at Welhunt

As low-carbon technologies move toward commercialization, the question of who bears the cost of the transition has also become critical. Chun-Te Tso (左峻德), Vice President of the Taiwan Institute of Economic Research (TIER), said CCUS could remain commercially attractive to technology companies with significant decarbonization needs if it can provide stable low-carbon power around the clock.

Pei-Ling Lu (呂佩玲), Chief Sustainability Officer of STARLUX Airlines (星宇航空) further expressed that SAF remains expensive and in limited supply, making it difficult for the aviation industry to absorb the entire cost through a single segment; costs must instead be shared across the supply chain. Carbon credits, meanwhile, are gradually becoming a transition cost for companies seeking international orders and compliance with market requirements.

From Green Power Procurement to Integrated Capabilities in "Energy, Carbon and Capital"

The common trend emerging from the 2-day forum is that corporate energy and net-zero strategies are entering a new stage.

In the AI era, companies must go beyond merely stating, "How much green power have we purchased?" They must ensure that they can secure reliable, low-carbon energy consistently. It is essential to convert decarbonization commitments into actionable, credible data and investment strategies. Furthermore, companies need to establish whether emerging low-carbon technologies can create cost structures and business models that the market demands and is ready to adopt.

The energy transition now spans a wide range of areas, including renewable energy development, marine engineering, microgrids, data centers, sustainability disclosure, transition finance, CCUS, and SAF. It is no longer an issue confined to a single technology or department. Instead, it has evolved into a comprehensive competition focused on the ability to integrate energy supply, carbon management, and capital allocation.

Methanol Qualified as a Feedstock for Sustainable Aviation Fuel

Claudia Hanisch Kommunikation

Fraunhofer-Institut für Solare Energiesysteme ISE

The more than 23,000 large aircraft worldwide consume approximately 350 billion liters of fuel annually and account for about 3 percent of human-caused CO2 emissions. For long-haul flights over 4,000 km in particular, there is no alternative to liquid fuels, as only these provide a sufficiently high energy density. The development of sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) has now reached an important milestone: Following successful qualification by the international standardization organization ASTM, methanol has been recognized as an approved feedstock for the alcohol-to-jet production pathway.

This means that in the future, methanol-to-jet blending components can be produced and mixed with at least 50 percent by volume of conventional kerosene to create a “drop-in” fuel—one that is fully compatible and can be used without any modifications to aircraft, engines, or existing infrastructure.

This decision marks a significant milestone for the “SAFari” collaborative project, which is funded by the Federal Ministry of Transportation. It was published on July 30, 2026, with the revision of the international specification ASTM D7566 Annex 5. The project aims to develop an efficient production process for sustainable aviation fuel based on methanol, thereby providing another technological building block for the decarbonization of aviation.

Throughout the multi-year project, the project partners closely supported the ASTM qualification process as members of the Methanol-to-Jet Task Force. The findings from the evaluation process were thus incorporated into the project work at an early stage and taken into account in the development of the production process. In this context, the early assessment of fuel quality was a key indicator of the project’s success. Since only small quantities of fuel were initially available during this development phase, the prescreening method developed at the DLR Institute of Combustion Technology was employed. It enables a comprehensive evaluation of fuel quality even with small sample quantities and provides an early assessment of whether a fuel meets the requirements of the ASTM specification. The results were immediately incorporated into process and catalyst development and helped ensure that the methanol-to-jet (MTJ) blending components developed in the project were specifically tailored to meet the anticipated international specification requirements.

Sustainable Methanol as the Basis for a New Aviation Fuel

SAF production based on MTJ technologies uses sustainable methanol derived from biogenic sources or produced from hydrogen and captured CO₂. In the methanol-to-olefins (MTO) synthesis, this methanol is converted into short-chain olefins, with water—a byproduct—removing the oxygen from the process. The short-chain olefins are then combined in an oligomerization process to form long-chain olefins, resulting in a product mixture that is liquid at room temperature. Through hydrogenation with hydrogen, the olefins are converted into stable paraffins. The result is a fuel blend that meets the aviation industry’s stringent requirements.

“In the SAFari project, we are working with our partners to develop an innovative process that aims to achieve a carbon-based SAF yield of over 85 percent by weight through customized catalysts and in-process recycling of material streams and heat. “With the successful completion of the ASTM qualification process, one of the biggest hurdles for demonstration and scaling has now been overcome,” explains Dr. Elias Frei, Head of the Hydrogen Technologies Division at Fraunhofer ISE.

“Following the successful ASTM qualification, the project is now focusing on further optimizing and scaling up the manufacturing process,” says Dr. Achim Schaadt, Head of the Sustainable Synthesis Products Division, looking ahead. “The goal is to produce larger quantities of fuel in order to conduct further research and demonstrations, thereby paving the way for the industrial implementation of methanol-based Sustainable Aviation Fuel,” adds Dr. Franz Mantei, project manager of the SAFari project. The market potential for this technology is enormous: for European air traffic alone, the mandated quotas will result in approximately 40 million metric tons by 2050.

In addition to Fraunhofer ISE, the consortium for the SAFari project (“Sustainable Aviation Fuels based on Advanced Reaction and Process Intensification”) includes ASG Analytik-Service AG, BP Europa SE, Clariant Produkte (Deutschland) GmbH, the German Aerospace Center (DLR) (DLR), Technip Energies France S.A.S., Südzucker AG, the Federal Association of the German Aviation Industry (BDL), and Airbus Helicopters Deutschland GmbH. The consortium thus covers the entire value chain. The SAFari project has been funded by the Federal Ministry of Transport (BMV) since December 1, 2022, for a period of six years.

text:
Woodside Energy and Petróleos Mexicanos (PEMEX) will explore opportunities to expand oil and gas projects through a newly signed non-binding Memorandum of Understanding (MoU).

The MoU will allow analysis of potential opportunities for exploration and extraction of hydrocarbons in Mexico’s deepwater and will enable an exchange of technical knowledge, experience, and industry best practices in the oil and gas sector, the companies said in a release Sept. 3.

Woodside and PEMEX are jointly developing the Trion oil project about 180 km off Mexico’s coastline and 30 km south of the US-Mexico maritime border. The project, about 64% complete as of June 30, 2026, lies in the Perdido Fold Belt at depths in 2,500–2,600 m of water. Mexico’s first ultra-deepwater oil development, Trion is designed for 24 subsea wells connected to a new 100,000 b/d floating production unit (Tláloc) and 950,000-bbl floating storage and offloading unit (Chalchi). Through estimated total capital investment of $7.2 billion, the development is targeting 479 MMboe of best estimate (2C) contingent oil and gas with first oil targeted for 2028.

Woodside is operator at Trion with a 60% interest. PEMEX holds the remaining 40% interest. Trion field was discovered by PEMEX in 2012.

Bangchak Group is one of the key partners supporting “KMITL EXPO 2026 – Ladkrabang Exhibition 2026,” held to mark the 66th anniversary of King Mongkut’s Institute of Technology Ladkrabang (KMITL). Taking place at KMITL from September 1–6, 2026, under the theme “From Lab to Life,” the event brings research and innovation out of the laboratory and into real-world use through exhibitions, knowledge-sharing sessions, and a range of related activities.

Mr. Chaiwat Kovavisarach, Group Chief Executive Officer and President, Bangchak Corporation Public Company Limited, is a graduate of KMITL’s Faculty of Engineering and currently serves as an Honorary Member of the KMITL Council. He was selected as one of the “KMITL Next 100,” recognizing high-potential KMITL alumni, and was honored at the event. Mr. Chaiwat said, “At KMITL, learning does not stop in the classroom. Students roll up their sleeves, get their hands dirty, and gain true understanding through hands-on experience.”

The “From Bio Molecules to Future Mobility” exhibition traces the development of Bangchak Group’s bioenergy business in line with the From Lab to Life concept. It emphasizes that innovation must move beyond research to be tested, deployed, and scaled in practice, showing visitors how energy innovation can connect with everyday life while creating value for Thailand.

The journey began more than 20 years ago, when Bangchak Group drew on the royal initiatives of His Majesty King Bhumibol Adulyadej, on self-reliance and renewable energy to develop its businesses. The Group has since built expertise in biological feedstocks, production technologies, and infrastructure, enabling it to produce low-carbon fuels for air, road, and marine transport, including sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), green diesel or HVO, and B24 Marine Biofuel.

For the Expo, Bangchak Group supplied 1,000 liters of HVO produced in Thailand for use in the event’s shuttle vehicles. This marked the first real-world use in Thailand of domestically produced HVO.

The exhibition also presents the development of feedstock supply chains for the bioenergy business. These include the Ucollect Box, an automated purchasing and collection unit for used cooking oil, which channels the collected oil into the “Fry to Fly” program for use as SAF feedstock. It also features “Farm to Fly,” which researches and develops Pongamia as an energy crop to broaden Thailand’s renewable feedstock options. The exhibition further highlights the role of the Carbon Markets Club as a knowledge-exchange platform that builds understanding of greenhouse gas emissions reduction and carbon markets.

Following the opening ceremony on September 1, Professor Yodchanan Wongsawat, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation, visited the “From Bio Molecules to Future Mobility” exhibition. He was welcomed and guided through the exhibition by Mrs. Gloyta Nathalang, Senior Executive Vice President, Sustainability Management and Corporate Communications, Bangchak Corporation Plc., together with Bangchak Group executives and employees.

KMITL is assessing the event’s greenhouse gas emissions, while Bangchak Group is providing carbon credits to offset those emissions so that the event can be held as a Carbon Neutral Event. The Group is also providing Inthanin beverages in recyclable packaging to encourage the circular use of resources.

As part of the event’s knowledge-sharing activities, Mrs. Gloyta was invited to deliver a presentation titled “Bangchak Group x KMITL: Greenovation in Action – From Lab to Life.” Mr. Jirapat Yaovatsakul, Vice President, Frontier Technology & Bangchak Initiative and Innovation Center (BiiC), Bangchak Group, spoke on “Innovation in the Age of AI.”

Bangchak Group invites school and university students, families, and anyone interested to explore the exhibition and experience future energy innovations at “KMITL EXPO 2026 – Ladkrabang Exhibition 2026: From Lab to Life.” The event features more than 400 research and innovation projects across 10 pavilions, over 140 workshops, and open-house activities offered by 14 faculties, three colleges, and one campus. Admission is free through September 6, 2026, from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. at KMITL. For further information, visit https://expo.kmitl.ac.th.

description:

Two Imperatives for Export Scale India’s next phase should be built around two imperatives; India must first build a unified “India Green Molecules” certification system.

text:
For decades, India’s energy conversation was shaped by one uncomfortable truth: we were buyers in a market controlled by producers. We imported crude, absorbed global volatility and allowed geopolitical disruption to dictate domestic economics. Bioenergy is giving India the opportunity to reverse that equation, not incrementally, but structurally.

Ethanol Must Become a Trade Instrument

The country has already demonstrated what determined policy, assured offtake and industrial execution can accomplish. Till date the Ethanol Blended Petrol (EBP) Programme has substituted nearly 316 lakh metric tonnes of crude oil to date, saved ₹1.97 lakh crore of foreign exchange, reduced approximately 952 lakh metric tonnes of CO2 emissions and paid about ₹1.66 lakh crore directly to farmers. pib.gov

This is not merely the success of a fuel-blending programme. It is proof that India can build a national clean-energy market at scale. Installed ethanol capacity has subsequently risen from 421 crore litres in 2014 to about 2,000 crore litres in 2026. Source

Capacity now exceeds immediate domestic absorption by an estimated 700 crore litres, a situation that should be understood not as oversupply but as export readiness. Source

The central question, therefore, is not whether India can make more ethanol. The question is whether India is prepared to turn ethanol into a strategic trade instrument, one that supports regional energy security, unlocks new revenue for farmers and establishes Indian producers as trusted suppliers of low-carbon fuel.

The global market is opening precisely where India has built capability. Countries across South Asia, Africa and Southeast Asia are pursuing higher ethanol blends but lack India’s combination of feedstock diversity, distillation capacity, blending experience and policy maturity. India must not wait for these markets to mature on their own. It should shape them through fuel-supply partnerships, blending support, common technical standards and long-term offtake arrangements.

The most important distinction is between exporting a commodity and exporting confidence. A litre of fuel that arrives without a credible carbon record will face price pressure. A litre that is traceable to sustainable feedstock, independently verified for

lifecycle emissions and delivered through dependable logistics will command strategic value. India has already enabled the export of 2G ethanol derived from non-food lignocellulosic feedstock, subject to authorisation, feedstock certification and quality compliance. Sourceapeda

From Residue to Strategic Resource

This creates an opening that goes far beyond conventional fuel trade. Agricultural residues, bagasse, forestry residues and organic waste can become inputs for advanced ethanol, sustainable aviation fuel and bio-based chemicals. The opportunity is to make every tonne of residue part of an organised industrial value chain rather than leaving it as an unmanaged agricultural externality.

Two Imperatives for Export Scale

India’s next phase should be built around two imperatives; India must first build a unified “India Green Molecules” certification system. Ethanol, CBG, sustainable aviation fuel, green methanol, green ammonia and hydrogen cannot evolve as disconnected policy silos. A single, credible national framework for feedstock traceability, lifecycle carbon accounting, sustainability verification and digital certificates of origin is essential. Every exported molecule must carry an environmental passport that gives an international buyer the same confidence in its carbon credentials as in its price, quality and delivery schedule.

Equally important, India must create bioenergy export corridors rather than stand-alone projects. A distillery, CBG plant or hydrogen facility does not become globally competitive at the factory gate. Competitiveness is created by the ecosystem around it: assured biomass aggregation, preprocessing clusters, efficient rail and road logistics, storage capacity, gas-grid access, blending infrastructure, port terminals and shipping partnerships. India should identify high-potential green-molecule corridors that connect agricultural belts and industrial clusters with coastal export gateways, converting dispersed capacity into a globally competitive supply chain.

CBG and Green Hydrogen: The Renewable Gas Advantage

CBG gives this vision greater depth. India’s CBG blending obligation begins at 1% of

CNG and PNG consumption in FY 2025-26, and expected to reach 5% by FY29. Source India had around 170 operating CBG plants in 2025, with nearly 300 more

under construction; output could grow more than sevenfold by 2030 under an

enabling policy pathway. Source

While, the immediate purpose of CBG is import substitution, cleaner mobility and

rural value creation. Its longer-term significance is even greater. Pipeline-quality biomethane, backed by credible renewable-gas certificates, can make India a supplier of environmental attributes and low-carbon gas solutions to markets where decarbonisation mandates are becoming commercially binding.

Green hydrogen completes the strategic picture. Current programmes support 3 GW per year of electrolyser manufacturing, 862 kilotonnes per year of green-hydrogen output, 724 kilotonnes per year of green-ammonia demand and 30 kilotonnes per year of hydrogen demand from refineries. Source This is how India builds an export portfolio that moves from liquid biofuels to renewable gas and, ultimately, to industrial decarbonisation. enerdata

Modern bioenergy already accounts for 13% of India’s total final energy consumption and is projected to grow by as much as 45% between 2023 and 2030. Source India’s task is to ensure that this growth does not remain a domestic story. We must turn it into an industrial and trade proposition of global consequence.iea

In a nutshell, the future will not belong merely to countries that produce energy. It will belong to countries that can produce verified, competitive and scalable green molecules. India has built the feedstock base, the industrial muscle and the policy momentum. The next step is to convert that strength into export leadership confidently, credibly and at scale.

Global sustainable fuels technology company Axens has been selected by Canada-based Expander Energy Inc. to provide its advanced Fischer-Tropsch (FT) Liquid Upgrading technology for projects aimed at producing sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) from cellulosic biomass, AlchemPro reported.

The technology will support Expander’s patented Enhanced Biomass to Liquids (EBTL) and Biomass Electrolysis to Liquids (BETL) processes, which are designed to convert cellulosic feedstocks into drop-in, second-generation fuels, including SAF.

The first deployments are planned at two commercial projects in Canada — the Wheatland Bio-Synfuels Facility near Calgary, Alberta, and the Mackenzie Biomass Derived E-Fuels Facility in northern British Columbia.

Both projects are progressing through regulatory and financing milestones, with final investment decisions targeted for December 2026.

Expander has also selected Axens as its strategic upgrading technology provider for a broader portfolio of SAF and renewable diesel developments. The partnership is aimed at scaling commercially viable pathways for producing lower-carbon aviation fuels from biomass.

Tina Craft, CEO of Axens Americas, said the company would support the growing adoption of second-generation fuels by leveraging its hydro-upgrading portfolio and expertise in advanced fuel production.

Gord Crawford, President and CEO of Expander Energy, said Axens’ technology would help ensure that the final-stage processing of the company’s Bio-SynJet sustainable aviation fuel meets the technical specifications required by the aviation industry.

The projects could provide an additional pathway for SAF production by using cellulosic biomass as a feedstock, supporting efforts to reduce the aviation sector’s dependence on conventional fossil-based jet fuel.

text:
US clean energy infrastructure company Avnos has commissioned a direct air capture (DAC) plant with capacity to capture 450 tonnes of carbon dioxide (CO2) per year while producing around 475,000 gallons of clean water.

Co-located with its technology development centre in Bridgewater, New Jersey, the demonstration plant will test Avnos’ hybrid DAC platform and generate operational data to support future commercial deployments.

Known as Project Brighton, it will also support Avnos’ work to demonstrate DAC-sourced CO2 for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) production.

The project is backed by the US Office of Naval Research (ONR), under a contract awarded to Avnos’ wholly owned subsidiary IWVC.

Using low-grade waste heat, Avnos’ hybrid DAC technology produces clean water and captures CO2 in a single process. It also claims the platform can be integrated with data centres, carbon storage hubs, and next-generation fuel production to address energy, water, and carbon challenges.

With Project Brighton operational, Avnos will continue to develop its commercial-scale facility Project Cedar, targeting the start of operations for early 2027.

Project Cedar will deploy four hybrid DAC modules to capture 3,000 tonnes of CO2 and produce over 6,000 tonnes of clean water each year, representing a significant increase in carbon capture capacity.

It is backed by a phased project financing agreement worth $17m with energy firms Shell US and Mitsubishi Americas.

Demand for CO2 is expected to rise significantly. By 2050, global industries could require up to six gigatonnes of CO2 annually as a feedstock for fuels, chemicals and materials.

Amid the global AI scale-up, data centres are also requiring increasing amounts of water. According to a new study from United Nations University (UNU), AI-related water consumption could equal the basic annual domestic needs of 1.3 billion people by 2030.

text:
The Philippines is considering raising its ethanol blending requirement to 15% from the current 10% as the government explores cheaper and more diversified feedstock to expand domestic bioethanol production, according to a report by Philstar.

The Departments of Agriculture and Energy are examining how existing ethanol distilleries can increase output without significantly raising production costs. A key part of the plan is to diversify the raw materials used for bioethanol production beyond conventional sugarcane-based feedstock.

Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. and Energy Secretary Sharon Garin recently discussed the use of molasses, sugarcane juice, locally produced corn and palm oil, as well as ways to utilise idle distillery capacity.

The government believes that securing cheaper feedstock could make domestic bioethanol more competitive with imported fuel while supporting local farmers and related industries. Lower production costs could also eventually help reduce gasoline prices, according to Tiu Laurel.

Corn is among the feedstock options being examined, with the Agriculture Department planning to increase production through improved seeds, mechanisation and contract farming arrangements with ethanol plants. However, Tiu Laurel said commercial viability would depend on ethanol producers being able to source corn at competitive prices.

Palm oil is also being assessed as a potential feedstock for bioethanol and sustainable aviation fuel, although new plantations could take around three years to mature.

Sugarcane-based feedstock currently accounts for an estimated 325 million to 385 million litres of bioethanol production annually, compared with an existing industry capacity of more than 500 million litres.

The Philippine government is also finalising national bioethanol standards, with the draft currently undergoing public consultation. Diversifying feedstock and improving the utilisation of existing capacity could help support a higher blending mandate while reducing dependence on any single agricultural commodity.

text:
Carbogenics USA is pleased to announce that it has officially secured its first production facility in Raton, New Mexico, marking a major milestone in the early-stage company’s growth and its ambition to build a regional hub for sustainable carbon innovation.

Established in 2025 as a separate U.S. company from its more-established Scottish parent, Carbogenics USA is building its own manufacturing, commercial and technical presence in New Mexico, while drawing on the technology and expertise developed by Carbogenics in Scotland.

The company’s growth in New Mexico has been supported by the Technology & Innovation Office, a division of Economic Development New Mexico, including Carbogenics USA’s receipt of a $440,000 Advanced Energy Award in 2025. This state support has played an integral role in helping the early-stage company establish its operations and progress plans for local manufacturing in New Mexico.

The new Raton facility will manufacture engineered carbon materials using locally sourced biomass, supporting applications across anaerobic digestion, water treatment, carbon removal and environmental remediation.

The announcement follows a period of rapid development for Carbogenics USA, including expansion of its local team and the development of strategic relationships with organizations across the state.

The Raton facility has been selected not only for its strategic location but also for its proximity to abundant biomass resources and leading research institutions. Carbogenics USA is working to strengthen collaborations with prospective partners including New Mexico State University (NMSU), The University of Texas at El Paso (UTEP), Vermejo Estate, St. Cloud Mining, and a growing network of industrial and utility organizations across New Mexico and Texas.

Together, these relationships have the potential to support the development of new engineered carbon materials using regional resources to address local environmental challenges, including water treatment and resource security.

The facility is expected to begin producing CreChar in the coming weeks, providing North American customers with locally manufactured engineered biocarbons designed to improve anaerobic digestion stability, safety and efficiency, while laying the foundations for future products across the wider Carbogenics carbon solutions platform.

Creating local value

Carbogenics USA’s approach is centered on creating value from regional resources.

By converting low-value biomass into high-performance engineered carbon materials, the company aims to strengthen domestic supply chains and contribute to cleaner water, renewable energy production and long-term carbon management.

The investment also represents an important step towards developing innovative, US-manufactured alternatives to imported activated carbons for environmental applications.

“Carbogenics is exactly the kind of investment Raton needs – new local jobs paired with a mission to turn our region’s wildfire risk into economic opportunity. We’re proud to welcome them to our community.” – Lori Chatterley, Mayor of Raton
